1.4.11 Subsequently, the Committee sought to know about any recent shift in paradigm and 
philosophy of working of the Department and to the extent the same is in consonance with 
global trend of health research. In response submitted as under:- 
 
1)   The paradigm shift in philosophy of working - 
 
a. Reassignment of roles: -Roles of different bodies under DHR including ICMR 
have been explicitly differentiated according to comparative advantage. DHR has 
retained stewardship functions—research infrastructure, human resource 
development and governance frameworks. Centre for Guidelines has been set up for 
Evidence synthesis, and Health Technology Assessment in India (HTAIn) attached 
office is established for cost effectiveness studies. ICMR has been aligned primarily 
to generation of research evidence through intramural and extramural mechanisms. 
 
b. From problem description to solution orientation: - The most visible doctrinal 
shift is the inversion of the research mix. Translational research now accounts for 
~70% of the portfolio compared with ~30% earlier.  
 
c. From centralized science to distributed capacity:- Extramural funding has 
expanded from 26% (2017) to 64% (2024) of the ICMR budget. Dedicated 
governance through an Additional DG (Extramural) and mission programmes such 
as the National Health Research Programme have made multi-centric, multi-state 
implementation the norm rather than the exception. 
 
d. From investigator autonomy to priority alignment: - Competitive intramural 
grants and structured review processes have shifted emphasis from individual 
curiosity-driven proposals toward institutional and national priorities. 
 
2) Instruments that operationalize the shift- The philosophical change is backed by   
machinery. 
a. Mission-mode research:- The National Health Research Programme organizes 
large, multi-disciplinary projects across priority areas—child health, cancers, 
anemia, mental health, AMR, vector-borne diseases, tuberculosis, maternal and 
elderly health, emergency care, and health systems. The design spans discovery to 
delivery. 
b. Innovation pathway support:- Through partnership with Central Drugs 
Standard Control Organization, the MedTechMitra platform provides regulatory 
navigation, mentoring, and evaluation. Quantitatively, hundreds of innovators have 
engaged; technologies have moved into test licensing, clinical evaluation, and HTA 
referral. 
c. Patent facilitation, infrastructure sharing (I-RISE), collaborating centres of 
excellence, and device fabrication capacity (e.g., mPRAGATI at Indian Institute of 
Technology Delhi) collectively reduce barriers between lab insight and market entry. 
d. Evidence architecture:- Creation of a Centre for Evidence-Based Guidelines, 
nationwide technical hubs, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses embeds 
methodological rigor into national recommendations. 

10 
 
e. Health Technology Assessment;-HTAIn’s formal positioning within DHR, 
expansion of resource hubs and centres, and completion of dozens of studies create 
an economic and outcomes-based filter for adoption. 
f. Human capital pipeline:- The HRD consolidation, fellowship expansion, 
women scientist awards, Young Medical Faculty PhD programme, and Faculty of 
Medical Research under Academy of Scientific and Innovative Research represent 
structural investment in physician-scientists. 
g. Pandemic preparedness & One Health:- Under DHR leadership, integrated 
surveillance, BSL-3 networking, mock drills, genomic concepts such as I-COG, and 
vaccine/diagnostic pipelines show a move toward anticipatory capability. 
h. Data as infrastructure:- The national repository introduces standardized, 
privacy-screened, reusable datasets to accelerate secondary research. 
i. Financial efficiency:- Utilization of 99.75% of allocation in 2024-25 indicates 
high absorptive and execution capacity. 
3)  Consonance with global trends in health research 
The described reforms to widely recognized directions in contemporary international 
practice: 
(i) emphasis on translation and impact, 
(ii) mission-driven consortia, 
(iii) regulatory and commercialization facilitation, 
(iv) HTA-anchored reimbursement logic, 
(v) One Health security frameworks, 
(vi) data platforms enabling reproducibility, and 
(vii) cultivation of clinician-scientists. 
 
Further, DHR also stated that it largely operates in line with Management by Objectives 
(MBO) through its schemes, guidelines, and attached offices to translate mission goals into 
programs with defined outputs (MRU/MRHRU labs, HRD schemes, grant-in aid, HTAIn, 
evidence‑based guidelines), which is characteristic of objective‑driven management in 
healthcare administration. 
1.4.12 The Committee is appreciative of the working ecosystem of DHR. Reassignment 
of roles, problem description to solution orientation, centralized science to distributed 
capacity are effective management tactics. Further, the Committee finds that operation 
mechanism for these tactics like mission-mode research, patent facilitation, Health 
Technology Assessment, human capital pipeline, data as infrastructure are bringing in 
expected benefits at ground level. The Committee also notes that the Department 
operates through the concept of Management by Objectives (MBO). This management 
approach is based on setting specific and measurable goals and, according to the 
Committee, is an effective requirement in healthcare administration. 
1.5 Health Research Challenges In India       
 
1.5.1 Health Research in India has covered many milestones in the last few decades. Still 
challenges are in abundance, primary being dearth in skilled work force, followed by the 
need to translate research findings into evidence-based practices; development and safe usage 
of emerging technologies, like AI; analyzing the various ethical component of research; etc.  

11 
 
 
1.5.2 As part of understanding these challenges, the Committee sought the details of the 
efforts made by DHR to ensure that research findings are consistently translated into 
evidence-based practices and implemented across all states, addressing the current policy-to-
practice gap. In reply, the Department submitted that Health Technology Assessment in India 
(HTAIn) has been established to systematically collect and analyse the evidence on cost, 
clinical effectiveness and safety of health interventions. By collaborating closely with State 
Health Departments, HTAIn facilitates capacity building, identifies regional priorities, and 
aids evidence-based decision-making by evaluating both clinical efficacy and cost-
effectiveness. HTAIn has provided strategic recommendations for a diverse range of 
community health interventions and diagnostic technologies like: 
 
i. Chronic Disease Screening: Screening of Type-2 diabetes, hypertension, and oral 
cancer. 
ii. Infectious Disease Management: Screening of Hepatitis B and C. 
iii. Indigenous Diagnostic Innovations: Locally developed Point of Care (PoC) test 
kits for Hemophilia A, Von Willebrand Disease (VWD), and Sickle Cell Disease. 
iv. Community-Based Technologies: 
a) Neonatal Care: Portable automated ABR devices for newborn hearing 
screenings. 
b) Respiratory Health: Handheld X-ray devices and AI-driven interpretation 
tools for the detection of Tuberculosis in field settings. 
 
1.5.3 Apart from HTAIn, DHR also has a Centre for Evidence Based Guidelines to 
promote consistency and methodological rigor in evaluating evidence for national health 
guidelines. Further, DHR plays a crucial role in mainstreaming implementation research to 
facilitate the promotion and implementation of research within its partner institutions which 
involves capacity building, co-production and community engagement, structured evaluation 
and monitoring and dissemination to policymakers. District-level tools such as risk 
stratification systems and dashboards are being tested in partnership with State Governments 
to improve outcomes. DHR has supported direct programme evidence generation, including 
development of operational guidelines for IV iron use in pregnancy, review and refinement 
of Anaemia Mukt Bharat (AMB) strategies, and updating treatment algorithms for anaemia 
in pregnant women and children. Under AMB multi-state PRAKASH study, ASHAs and 
frontline workers have also been involved in routine programme settings to generate 
actionable evidence, and the findings are systematically shared with states and M/o HFW 
through structured feedback mechanisms, enabling timely programme strengthening and 
closing the policy-to-practice gap. Further, the multi-state NECCTAR trial generates 
implementation-ready evidence by strengthening the nutritional quality of take-home rations 
alongside structured behaviour change interventions within existing government platforms, 
enabling States to directly adopt or adapt findings. Overall, DHR’s approach ensures that 
research outputs directly inform programme design, operational guidelines, and scale-up 
decisions, thereby, systematically bridging the evidence-to-implementation gap. 
 
1.5.4. According to DHR, there are several examples of research findings from MRHRUs 
that contributed to addressing the current policy to practice gap. These are as follows:  
 

12 
 
1. MRHRU Dahanu: Implemented a comprehensive programme in Dahanu Block 
covering prevention, early management, and surveillance of snakebite. Research contributed 
to WHO recognition of snakebite as a notifiable disease. 
 
2. MRHRU Chandragiri: Conducted a state-wide assessment of better diet program 
that focused on children from deprived settings in Andhra Pradesh Social Welfare 
Residential Educational Institutions Society. The findings have resulted in an informed 
policy revision in food package distribution practices.  
 
3. MRHRU Puducherry: Implemented a school-based dengue reduction programme 
combining education, awareness, and community participation. This has been recognized as 
a scalable inter-sectoral model for vector-borne disease prevention.  
 
4. MRHRU Tirunelveli: Developed an Android Applications for early stroke 
identification and adverse pregnancy outcomes by using Bateman’s Obstetric Comorbidity 
Index.  
 
5. MRHRU Tigiria: Developed the Demography Integrated Surveillance for Health 
Assessment (DISHA). This has facilitated real-time monitoring of dengue and chikungunya 
trends at the community level. 
 
1.5.5 The Committee recognises the work done by DHR through HTAIn and MRHRU 
towards systematic collection of data and analysis of evidence thereby addressing the 
current ‘policy to practice’ gap. Having said that, the Committee feels more can be 
done to track whether research findings are actually incorporated into 
national/state/district health policy/plans. The Committee observes the need and 
existence of programmes addressing malnutrition, infectious diseases, and maternal 
mortality point to this. Taking this into account, the Committee recommends that DHR 
should create an “Evidence-to-Action Dashboard” that maps research outputs against 
national health priorities. Further, every ministry/department involved in the 
implementation of a particular programme/scheme should submit an action-taken 
report on relevant ICMR/DHR studies within six months of its publication, with public 
disclosure and Parliamentary review. The Committee is of the considered view that 
such measures would bridge the critical translation gap and ensure that India’s robust 
health research ecosystem directly strengthens evidence-based community interventions 
and delivers measurable public health gains. The Committee is of the firm conviction 
that research must ultimately translate into affordable medicines and accessible 
therapies for citizens. 
 
1.5.6 Another concern area of Health Research is development of AI technologies/ tools 
and integration of digital health platforms into the existing public health system. One of the 
crucial steps in this direction is setting up ICMR-National Institute for Research in Digital 
Health and Data Science (NIRDHDS) and entrusting it with the task of developing India-
specific AI-based solutions for strengthening the healthcare system with an overarching goal 
of achieving Universal Health Coverage. The Committee wanted DHR to share a few 
flagship AI-based solutions or pilots that NIRDHDS has already deployed or is piloting in 
public health facilities. In response, the Department a few ongoing scientific works for

1.5.13 In this connection, the Department also brought to the notice of the Committee the 
main challenges in AI and Digital Health Integration which are as follows: 
 
(i) Data Quality, Privacy, and Security: AI models require vast amounts of high-quality, 
diverse, and representative data for training and validation. 
(ii) Regulatory and Ethical Concerns: The rapidly evolving nature of AI technology 
outpaces traditional regulatory frameworks for medical devices. 
(iii) Interoperability and Integration: A lack of standardised data protocols hinders 
effective data exchange between different systems and providers. 
(iv) Clinical Validation and Reliability: Rigorous, real-world validation through 
prospective studies and randomised controlled trials (RCTs) is needed to demonstrate 
a tool's clinical and economic utility and ensure it is safe and reliable for diverse 
populations. 
(v) Workforce Skills and Acceptance: There is a significant shortage of healthcare 
professionals with expertise in AI and data science. 
 
1.5.14 The Committee is pleased to note the work in progress towards the development 
of India-specific AI-based solutions for strengthening the healthcare system in the 
country. Having said that, the Committee feels that emerging technologies such as AI 
diagnostic tools and digital health platforms in India remain in their early stages due to 
issues like poor data management, algorithmic bias, ethical challenges, and limited 
internet access in semi-urban, rural, hilly and tribal areas. Alongwith these factors, the 
Committee also hold the view that callous electronic health records maintenance and 
cybersecurity vulnerabilities compromise trust and safety towards AI tools & digital 
health platforms. Accordingly, the Committee opine that there should be data driven 
healthcare planning with strict privacy safeguards. For the success of these data driven 
healthcare policy, the country also needs technology empowered scientist, doctors, 
support staff and patients consolidating Protective Research Equilibrium (PRE). 
 
1.5.15 As steps to make AI tools & digital health platforms more reliable the 
Committee recommends that DHR should make pre and post-market HTA mandatory 
for all AI diagnostics seeking to integrate with public health system. DHR must update 
and enforce Ethics Guidelines for Application of Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical 
Research and Healthcare, 2023 by ICMR with compulsory bias audits, diverse dataset 
requirements, and ‘Human-in-the-Loop’ features for every government funded or 
publicly integrated AI tool. Health data/record being a sensitive subject, the Committee 
recommends for more region-diseases specific studies by DHR/ICMR on health data 
bias, maintenance and usage. 
 
1.5.16 The Committee notices that inspite of Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission 
(ABDM), internet in rural/tribal areas is still unreliable. Another concern in rural area 
is digital literacy gaps and inadequate training for frontline workers like Accredited 
Social Health Activist (ASHAs) and Auxiliary Nurse Midwife (ANM).  This results in 
urban-centric development and continued exclusion of millions in the rural belts from 

16 
 
benefits of tools like AI-powered chest X-ray analysis or clinical decision support 
systems like eSanjeevani. To address these, the Committee recommends that DHR 
should develop offline-capable indigenous AI solutions and launch a nationwide AI 
training programme designed for last-mile integration beginning with the aspirational 
districts for frontline workers (ASHAs, ANMs) through Model Rural Health Research 
Units. 
 
1.5.17 On the sensitive issue of ethical concerns related to Health Research, DHR further

Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) and Anusandhan National Research Foundation 
(ANRF) to avoid duplication and ensure interoperability of datasets and AI models. 
NIRDHDS functions as a technical integrator and standards steward, aligning with IndiaAI 
on AI safety and evaluation, with ABDM/NHA on interoperable health data pipelines, and 
with national research funding frameworks, thereby minimising duplication, enabling reuse 
of public datasets, and ensuring interoperable, trustworthy AI development for health in 
India.  
 
1.5.18 The Committee further queried on the safeguard measures built into NIRDHDS 
projects to prevent re-identification of health & research data, especially when datasets are 
shared with private partners. In reply, DHR submitted that as of now, data has not been

constituted a technical working group on data curation, sharing &governance. The group is 
working on the preparation of standard guidelines and frameworks for data curation, 
anonymisation, and sharing pipelines. The work on the federated benchmarking platform for 
testing SI models in health with IIT Kanpur and NHA is a step towards creating a safe 
environment for model testing without giving data access to the model developers. Similarly, 
another federated model training platform is under development by iSpirit where developers 
can train their models on datasets without being able to see or retrieve data. Under the

is secure and accessible is being built. The institute has been targeting Anusandhan National

execution. The institute has been aligning central and state entities through standardised

1.5.19 It was also submitted that ICMR-NIRDHDS has initiated the work for development 
of an India-specific AI risk-classification framework for health through a dedicated “Risk, 
Monitoring & Evaluation” working group. This initiative is unique in that it proposes a risk-
tiered model linked to clinical use and potential patient harm, rather than technology type 
alone. The framework will establish lifecycle-based approval and oversight mechanisms and 
mandate standards for data quality, transparency, and bias mitigation for high-risk health AI 
systems.

field. However, like any technology, it comes with both advantages and challenges. In

2.3 The Committee finds that the public expenditure on health research has been 
maintained at a modest 0.02% of GDP and has contributed to the slow progress in the area of 
Health Research in the country. In this regard, the Committee wished to know from DHR the 
measures adopted by them to bridge the significant funding gap to support cutting-edge 
research and infrastructure development across the country.     
 
2.4 In response, the Department submitted that it has employed a multi-pronged approach 
to bridge the health research funding gap, primarily through fostering public-private 
partnerships, and implementing targeted grant-in-aid schemes for research and infrastructure 
development. The key initiatives are as under: 
 
i. Public-Private Partnerships (PPPs): DHR is actively promoting PPP models to 
augment infrastructure and expertise, encouraging private equity investments into 
underfunded segments of the healthcare system. 
ii. Inter-Sectoral Convergence Scheme: DHR provides grant-in-aid to encourage 
research partnerships among different government agencies, NGOs, and industry 
to translate existing health knowledge into deliverable products and processes. 

19 
 
iii. During the 15th Finance Commission (FC) period, an allocation of Rs 324 crore 
was made for the VRDL Scheme. For the 16th FC period, the DHR has proposed 
Rs 980.91 crore, which includes an expanded scope covering syndromic 
surveillance activities, recurring support to Infectious Disease Research and 
Diagnostic Laboratories (IRDLs), and the establishment of new VRDLs, among 
other initiatives. If the proposed allocation is approved, there would be sufficient 
funding to support cutting-edge research and infrastructure development under the 
VRDL Scheme, effectively bridging the current funding gap. 
iv. Multidisciplinary Research Units (MRUs): DHR continues to establish and fund 
MRUs in government medical colleges and research institutions across the 
country. These units aim to strengthen health research infrastructure, build 
capacity, and focus research on national priorities like non-communicable 
diseases (NCDs). 
v. Model Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs): To bridge the urban-rural 
research gap, MRHRUs are being established in the vicinity of 
Primary/Community Health Centres. These units focus on transferring technology 
to the rural level and improving health services for the rural population. 
vi. Human Resource Development (HRD) Scheme: This initiative aims to create a 
pool of talented health research personnel through fellowships, scholarships, and 
specialized training for medical faculty, mid-career scientists, and students in 
priority areas such as clinical trials, genomics, and stem cell research. 
 
2.5 Further, DHR-ICMR 2024-29 Action Plan directed research toward critical national 
health challenges: promoting indigenous and affordable health technologies, providing 
solutions for difficult health problems like anaemia, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and 
child malnutrition, advancing digital health solutions and technology-driven surveillance, 
ensuring research evidence is translated into practical action and policy.  
 
2.6 The Committee also sought to know the specific steps DHR has been taking to ensure 
better utilization of allocated capital funds to develop tangible healthcare assets and research 
facilities. In reply, the Department stated the following: 
 
i. Improved Financial Discipline: DHR has emphasised adhering to financial 
discipline and administrative due diligence as outlined in GFRs. 
ii. DHR ensures that key projects and programmes are sufficiently funded based on 
the initial budgetary allocations and plans to approach the Ministry of Finance for 
additional funds at the Revised Estimate (RE) stage and through supplementary 
grants, if necessary, depending on the progress of ongoing missions, R&D 
projects, and facility build-up. 
iii. The Department is actively involved in building new infrastructure and 
establishing state-of-the-art equipment. This includes the establishment of a 
network of Viral Research and Diagnostic Laboratories (VRDLs) for managing 
epidemics and pandemics, development of Multi-Disciplinary Research Units 
(MRUs) in government medical colleges and Model Rural Health Research Units 
(MRHRUs) in rural areas. 
iv. The Government of India conceptualized and introduced an umbrella scheme for 
development of Infrastructure for health research since 2013-14.  It has 02 sub-

20 
 
schemes namely (i) establishing Multidisciplinary Research Units (MRUs) in 
Medical Colleges/Research Institutes, and (ii) establishing Model Rural Health 
Research Units (MRHRUs) in rural areas. While MRUs are established in a 
Medical College, MRHRUs are standalone buildings in vicinity of a Community 
Health Centre/Primary Health Centre.  Both the sub-schemes promote creation of

v. To ensure effective utilisation of capital support provided under the Viral Research

2.7 The Committee observes that since Government is spending only 0.02% of GDP 
for Health research for the last 5 years, a large proportion of existing schemes would 
naturally suffer from implementation gaps, poor last-mile delivery, and suboptimal 
progress in semi-urban, rural, hilly and tribal areas. Despite the funds being hard to 
come, DHR has always ensured best utilization of the allocated funds and the 
Committee is appreciative of the efforts of DHR. Having said that, the Committee 
believes that the shortfall in Health Research Funding is not only a budgetary issue but 
reflects weak evidence on the returns of existing schemes/programmes as well, both 
physical and financial. DHR should be able to persuade the Ministry of Finance in pre-
budget consultations, that every additional fund allocated, yields promotion of 
indigenous affordable health technologies and digital health solutions which is 
translated into practical health policies and actions, all of these ultimately translating to 
saving of public funds. Accordingly, the Committee recommends a dedicated cell in 
DHR to bring forth periodic reports on both the physical and financial aspects of public 
health spending on bio-medical research. The reports should give emphasis on the 
outcome of schemes/programmes and utility of innovations and technology emanating 
from bio medical research for practical use on the ground level. 
 
2.8 To improve the fund utilization of DHR, the Committee recommends measures 
like teaming of seasoned scientists with early-career researchers in 
programmes/schemes to bridge knowledge gaps and variant insights in the funding 
landscaping, real-time tracking of projects outcomes involved in assets creation via 
GIS-enabled portal, developing scorecards and linking the same to annual performance 
appraisals of institutes/individuals concerned, introduction of automatic forfeiture and 
reallocation of unutilised capital grants after a certain period as well as blacklisting of 
defaulting institutes for future projects. For the Committee, the success of any research 
endeavour is inextricably linked to adequate funding. By addressing the challenges 
inherent in the funding process through these recommended methods, DHR should be 
able to strengthen their position which may catalyse the Ministry of Finance to dedicate 

21 
 
more funds for the Department for the stated strategic purpose based on actual 
outcome intending to make the healthcare more accessible and affordable. 
 
2.9 Regarding the issue of only less than 25% of the health and education cess collections 
being transferred to the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Nidhi (PMSSN) and its 
consequences on DHR-funded schemes, the Department replied that its schemes are not 
directly funded by the PMSSN. But the Department expressed its concern that its 
schemes/programmes are part of the larger health ecosystem that experiences increased 
financial pressure when the dedicated cess funds are not fully utilised as intended. This can 
lead to greater competition for limited Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) funds, potentially 
hindering the DHR's ability to secure increased funding for expanding its research initiatives 
and human resource development programmes. 
 
2.10 The Committee understands that currently DHR schemes are not benefitting 
from by the Pradhan Mantri Swasthya Suraksha Nidhi (PMSSN). However, the 
Committee is of the firm opinion that the DHR schemes are in no way less important in 
the endeavours to attain inter- alia the targets of National Health Policy, 2017, which is 
one of the salient features of PMSSN. Hence, the Committee recommends that DHR 
should submit a formal proposal to the Ministry of Finance for ring-fencing an 
appropriate percentage of the health component of cess from PMSSN for its schemes/ 
programmes. The Committee feels that such a proposal would hold weightage since 
PMSSN is the primarily a non-lapsable reserve fund which has been conceived to cover 
broader aims like National Health Policy 2017, Emergency & Disaster preparedness 
and response during health emergencies, etc. These aims of PMSSN directly impinge 
implementation of evidence-based interventions in urban/rural/tribal areas and 
translation of research outcomes into policy and practice.

financial support to medical colleges, universities and research institutions across the

geographical location of an institution does not limit the population coverage of research 
activities.  Available data indicates that nearly 60% of ongoing research projects are funded 
in institutions situated in Tier II and Tier III cities. Furthermore, many studies conducted by 
institutions located in urban areas involve extensive field components covering both rural and

ensure representation across geographical regions, including urban, rural and remote 
communities.

Diseases, ICMR-Regional Medical Research Centre Sri Vijaya Puram and ICMR-Regional 
Medical Research Centre Bhubaneswar. These institutes generate evidence on disease 
burden, nutrition, maternal and child health, genetic disorders and health-system 

22 
 
strengthening among tribal populations, including Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups

for health research.  It has two sub-schemes namely (i) establishing Multidisciplinary 
Research Units (MRUs) in Medical Colleges/Research Institutes, and (ii) establishing Model 
Rural Health Research Units (MRHRUs). The MRUs are predominantly located in urban 
areas and MRHRUs are located in rural areas. The allocation of funds for the two sub-

 2.13 The Committee considers the submission of the Department that as far as 
research programmes/schemes are concerned, even though institutions are generally 
located in Tier I, II and III cities, the population coverage of research activities and 
field components includes both rural and underserved populations. Also, the 
submission made by the Department of 60% and 40% fund allocation to MRUs and 
MRHRUs respectively, under Development of Infrastructure for Health Research 
during the 15thFinance Commission Period suggests appropriately earmarked funding 
pattern for both urban and rural belts. Still the Committee feels that lack of proper 
monitoring mechanism when research is conducted in rural areas leads to 
infrastructure and human resource gaps at the time of its implementation. To address 
this, DHR can launch a real-time portal linked to all MRHRUs and Ayushman Bharat 
Health & Wellness Centres (AB-HWCs) and accessible to the Centre and States. 
Moreover, to bring in more transparency in fund allocation, the Committee 
recommends mapping of funding patterns and to make available in public domain, 
institute-wise, State-wise, and rural/urban break-up data of sanctioned funds. Further, 
an independent annual equity audit by CAG should be institutionalised, with findings 
presented to the Parliament. 
 
2.14 The Committee is of the considered view that when research funding remains 
concentrated in urban-based institutions and research centres it may result in health 
challenges innate to rural and tribal areas such as vector-borne diseases, malnutrition, 
maternal mortality and sickle cell anaemia, not getting its needed share of funding. 
More research institutions in the tribal and aspirational districts will ensure the area 
specific research gets needed attention and no region is left behind in healthcare 
preparedness. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that DHR should notify a 
policy mandating that at least 40% of all extramural research grants be awarded to 
projects led by or implemented in rural/tribal institutions. These projects can also be 
partnered by State Medical Colleges and Model Rural Health Research Units 
(MRHRUs).  
 
2.15 As perceived by the Committee, another downside for rural and tribal areas is 
that their medical colleges and research units lack trained manpower, equipment, and 
administrative support, making them less competitive for DHR grants thereby 
reinforcing the urban funding dominance. In this regard, the Committee recommends 

23 
 
that DHR should provide extra weightage in grant evaluation for proposals from these 
institutions and special incentives like hardship allowance, fast-track promotion for 
scientists opting for rural postings to aggressively handhold them.

targeted scaling of new initiatives, MedTechMitra, First-in-the-World, Centre for 
Advanced Research (CAR), National Health Research Priority Projects (NHRP), 
NIRMAN, National Virus Resource Facility (NVRF), etc.) and HRD fellowships. The 
Committee expects DHR to devise proactive steps to efficiently utilise the increased 
funding received for the ensuing year. Ensuring the assessment of capacity to utilise 
including institutional infrastructure, financial compliance, project progress roadmap, 
etc,this should be ensured before funds are released. Such measures would be especially 
pivotal in case of new Schemes like MedTechMitra, Patent Mitra, etc. The key concerns 
areas of utilisation leading to under absorption of resources that needs to be identified 
and sorted out. The Committee also strongly favours and recommends the creation of 
an institutional mechanism to monitor progress of GIA and PM-ABHIM projects, 
which have consistently witnessed project delays in the past. Realtime Outcome 
Dashboards would be a great tool for the purpose of monitoring the schemes. This step 
may be in addition to the time proven, periodic utilisation review mechanisms that may 
be in place for expected results. A dedicated monitoring mechanism would help to 
convert the ₹200+ crore GIA-Capital spike into tangible assets within the financial year, 
avoiding RE-stage surrenders and supporting long-term research capacity.

allocated, the Department may explore channelising money from schemes making 
sluggish progress, despite best efforts, to schemes making better headway. The 
Committee recommends such move can be made when required with the due 
consultation and approval of the Ministry of Finance, wherever required. 
 
2.2.9 The Committee takes into account the submission of DHR about the proposed 
new research infrastructure activities under PM-ABHIM Scheme for the 16th Finance 
Commission period viz. NIRMAN, NVRF, National Grade Data Centre and Disaster 
Recovery Infrastructure and establishment of Infectious disease Research & Diagnostic 
Labs. All are critical initiatives that can act as stepping stones in the nation’s progress 
towards self-reliance in the health sector in combating its challenges.  
 
2.2.10 With regard to the capital expenditure (Rs 1.81crore) remaining negligible at less than 
0.04% of total allocation despite the overall increase in total allocation of DHR for 2026- 
2027, the DHR informed that the comparatively low capital expenditure of the Department 
amounting to approximately ₹1.75–1.81 crore in 2026–27 (less than 0.04% of the total 
allocation of ₹4821.21 crore), may appear disproportionate in isolation. However, it does not 
indicate any policy preference for revenue or grant-based spending at the cost of 
infrastructure development. DHR is primarily a policy, coordination and funding department 
under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare and does not maintain independent 
laboratory campuses or buildings. Accordingly, its direct capital outlay is limited to essential 
administrative requirements and is expected to be suitably adjusted at the Revised Estimates 
(RE) stage and in subsequent years as required. The creation and strengthening of physical 
research infrastructure is undertaken through the Indian Council of Medical Research 
(ICMR) and national health research missions, and therefore the bulk of capital formation is 
reflected under those programme heads rather than under the DHR administrative budget, 
including GIA (Capital) of ₹200 crore earmarked for the relocation and establishment of NIV 
Pune at Pashan, development of the Institute of Digital Health in Delhi NCR, infrastructure 
expansion at ICMR Headquarters along with ongoing construction across 28 institutes, 
establishment of a Data Centre at ICMR Headquarters, and procurement of essential 
equipment for 28 ICMR institutes and centres. 
2.2.11 Substantial investments are, in fact, being made towards strengthening national 
research capacity. Under the Human Resource and Capacity Development (HRCD) Umbrella 
Scheme of ICMR, an allocation of ₹105 crore for 2026–27 supports development of a trained 
health research workforce through Short-Term Studentships, medical thesis support, PhD and 
post-doctoral fellowships, women scientist schemes, training workshops and funding of 
ongoing research projects, with several hundred to more than a thousand fellowships being 
supported during the year. In addition, ₹24 crore has been provided for inter-sectoral 
convergence and research grants to promote development of new technologies and affordable 
healthcare solutions, and ₹21 crore for the DIAMONDS programme supporting 25 hubs and 
establishing new centres, along with international cooperation activities. Ongoing grant-in-
aid projects with national institutions such as CSIR laboratories, ICAR institutes and state 
medical colleges cover drug discovery, cancer therapeutics, pulmonary fibrosis, probiotics, 
chronic kidney disease biomarkers and treatment of kala-azar, thereby strengthening 
translational and collaborative research. 

27 
 
2.2.12 Further, significant infrastructure development is being undertaken under the PM-
Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-ABHIM) with an allocation of ₹221.32 
crore, including completion of zonal National Institute of Virology facilities, establishment 
of a BSL-3 laboratory at NITVAR Pune, creation of Infectious Disease Research and 
Diagnostic Laboratories, a Health Research Data Centre, the National Virus Resource 
Facility at NIV Pune and the National Initiative for Reliable Medical Device Testing and 
Assessment Network (NIRMAN).These initiatives substantially enhance national biosecurity 
preparedness, diagnostics, medical device evaluation and research capability. 
2.2.13 Therefore, the present budgetary pattern reflects a structured division of 
responsibilities: DHR focuses on policy guidance, funding support and human resource 
development, while ICMR and national missions undertake infrastructure creation and 
laboratory expansion. The approach emphasizes development of skilled human resources and 
a distributed national research network rather than centralised administrative infrastructure. 
In the long term, this model is expected to strengthen health research capacity, accelerate 
translational research, improve disease surveillance and pandemic preparedness and promote 
indigenous innovation. Accordingly, the low capital expenditure under DHR should be 
viewed as a matter of budgetary classification within an integrated national health research 
architecture and not as an indication of inadequate investment in research infrastructure. 
 
2.2.14 With respect to the matter of capital investment in health research, the 
Committee reckon from the submission of DHR that while DHR is primarily a policy, 
coordination and funding entity and do not maintain independent laboratory 
infrastructure. Physical research infrastructure is undertaken through ICMR and 
national health research missions which reflect the bulk of capital formation. PM-
ABHIM also involves significant infrastructure developments. Hence, the present 
budgetary pattern reflects a division of responsibilities between DHR and ICMR on 
these lines. The Committee makes the observation that DHR and ICMR shoulder a very 
significant component of national advancement that would contribute towards the 
Viksit Bharat vision of the Government and should take all measures to bring out the 
expected outcomes.

2.4.5 Second, the allocation mechanism may be strengthened through outcome-linked 
budgeting. DHR programmes such as diagnostic development, vaccine support, health-
technology assessment and public-health research directly influence affordability of care, 
reduction in disease burden and savings in public health expenditure. Systematic 
documentation of economic returns—such as cost savings to national health programmes, 
import substitution of medical technologies and support to indigenous manufacturing—can 
justify higher public investment in health research relative to traditional laboratory-based 
research sectors. 
2.4.6 Third, enhanced inter-ministerial convergence may be institutionalised. Creation of 
joint national missions for diagnostics, medical devices and clinical trials infrastructure may 
further strengthen this approach. DHR has already undertaken such initiatives. For example, 
Ayush - ICMR Centre for Integrative Health Research has been established as a joint 
initiative between the Ministry of Ayush and ICMR to generate robust scientific evidence on 
integrative and traditional medicine approaches through collaborative research, clinical 
studies, and policy guidance. Similarly, Med-Tech Mitra is a joint initiative by ICMR and 
Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) launched in December 2023. Over 
400 innovators, start-ups, and industry partners have been engaged through this platform 
helping them overcome challenges in the process of developing regulation compliant 
products, their clinical validation, and scaling-up.  
2.4.7 Fourth, a dedicated capital funding window for national health research infrastructure 
may be considered. While laboratory infrastructure is currently created through ICMR and 
national health missions, establishment of permanent national centres for clinical trials, 
regulatory science, health data analytics and evaluation of medical technologies would 
improve long-term institutional capacity and justify enhanced allocations. This may be 
complemented by public-private partnerships, especially for device testing facilities, bio-
banks and advanced laboratories. 
2.4.8 DHR’s HTAIn should be viewed as a prerequisite for efficient rollout of AB-PMJAY, 
National Health Mission, and national health programmes, and not as a discretionary research 
scheme. Evidence generation through it is a very small fraction of what it guides. Therefore, 
a fixed share of major centrally sponsored health schemes can be routed to HTAIn for 
evidence generation and budget impact analyses. 
2.4.9 Finally, strengthening translation and commercialization pathways may improve 
budget justification. Facilitating technology transfer, start-up incubation, and integration with 
the domestic pharmaceutical and medical device industry would demonstrate tangible 
economic benefits from health research investment. Evidence of improved programme 
efficiency, indigenous innovation, and reduced healthcare costs can support a case for 
progressively increasing the Department’s share within the national R&D expenditure. 
2.4.10 Already, DHR has proposed for Medical Innovations Development Acceleration 
Council (MIDAC) for steering translational research partnerships and technology 
development with focus on priority health conditions for the nation. It will support industry 
collaboration to bridge critical gaps in product development, assist researchers in validation 
and evaluation products and also manage royalty and equity for ICMR.  

32 
 
 
2.4.11  The Committee takes into account DHR's budgetary allocations for research 
activities vis-a-vis other key ministries and departments involved in research, such as 
the Department of Science and Technology (DST), Department of Biotechnology 
(DBT), Department of Space (DoS), Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), Ministry of 
Education and Ministry of AYUSH in the Union Budget 2026-27, is the lowest to DHR. 
Comparison of the similarly structured Ministry of Health & Family Welfare and 
Ministry of Education is more thought provoking, as both cater to infrastructural 
development as well as research. Even, Ministry of Education is spending 9% of its 
total allocation for research activities while Ministry of Health & Family Welfare 
shares only 4.8% with DHR. Having said that, the Committee observes that out of the 
total Government of India R&D outlay (all scientific ministries combined) for the FY 
2026–27 at ₹63,381 crore, DHR is allocated to the tune of Rs. 4,821.21 crore which is 
approximately 7.6%. When compared to 2017-18, the BE for the DHR/ICMR has more 
than tripled in 2026-27.However, the allocation over the years has been chequered. 
Whereas the growth in BE for CSIR/DSIR for the corresponding period has been 1.5 
times but their increase has been linear. 
 
2.4.12 Overall, the Committee feels that the DHR's share of budgetary allocations for 
research activities can be considered only as modest compared to other key ministries 
and departments involved in the field. Funding for the sake of enhanced budget 
allocation is not proper without relevant outcome. To improve/enhance its total 
allocation DHR has adopted many policy directions like recognition of health research 
as a strategic national priority comparable to sectors such as space, atomic energy and 
industrial research,  strengthening of allocation mechanism through outcome-linked 
budgeting, institutionalisation of enhanced inter-ministerial convergence, 
conceptualisation of a dedicated capital funding window for national health research 
infrastructure complemented by public-private partnerships, viewing of schemes like 
HTAIn as a prerequisite for efficient rollout of AB-PMJAY, National Health Mission, 
and national health programmes and not as a discretionary research scheme, etc. Also, 
DHR/ICMR should consider raising its own resources by tying up with major private 
players in the industry. The Committee is of the considered view that these policy 
directions of DHR can accelerate the pace of activities in the field of medical research in 
the country that would ultimately lead to global standard of healthcare. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that DHR should strive for Medical Innovations 
Development Acceleration Council (MIDAC) for steering translational research 
partnerships and technology development and equity for ICMR.

2.6.11 The Committee observes that as of February 2026, no new separate HTA 
Scheme has been publicly notified. As on date, the new HTA Scheme titled ‘Integrating 
Evidence-based Guidelines and Health Technology Assessment in Programme and 
Policy’ – 2026-27 to 2030-31 is awaiting final approval of Department of Expenditure. 
Whereas the old scheme HTAIn is continuing only as a sub-scheme under the umbrella 
Human Resource & Capacity Development programme of the 15thFinance Commission 
cycle. In this scenario, the Committee is apprehensive that this change over and absence 
of a dedicated, adequately funded HTA scheme risks funding gaps, stalled HTA studies, 
etc. The Committee, over the years, has repeatedly recommended for time-bound 
planning and better coordination while seeking approval to avoid administrative delays. 
In tune with this, keeping in mind the relevance of having HTA, the Committee 
recommends that the Department should approach the Department of Expenditure to 
expedite its approval and finalise a standalone National Health Technology Assessment 
Scheme considering the growing need for evidence-based prioritisation under national 
programmes like, Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, AB-HWCs, etc. 
 
2.6.12. The Committee is of the firm opinion that the Department should revisit the 
proposed outlay of Rs. 379 Cr, if a standalone National HTA scheme is to be considered 

40 
 
in place of a mere expansion of the existing HTAIn sub-scheme for 2026–31. Taking 
into consideration the trend of allocation, the Committee notices that the Department 
hardly gets its Projected Demand for a scheme because even for the FY 2026-27, the 
proposed demand of Rs. 56.63 Cr was downsized to Rs. 25.00 Cr. Percentage of 
Variation of BE 2026-27 as compared to Projected Demand was 55.85%. The 
Committee, therefore recommends the Department to be more realistic and reasonable 
while making projections in consonance with requirement and in convincing the 
Department of Expenditure of their fund requirement with due justification. 
 
2.6.13 The Committee appreciates that the targets set under Health Technology 
Assessment for the FY 2025-26 have exceeded the mark except for the fact that no of 
policy briefs have been utilized by user agencies. The Annual Report -2025-26 of DHR 
shows that HTAIn has completed 136 studies. But the need of the hour is also that these 
studies are consumed by user agencies in the form of guidelines, uptake of technology in 
program and for procurement of devices/kits/technologies. Only then India’s goal of 
Atmanirbhar Bharat in health technology can be achieved taking the nation towards 
efficient, equitable and sustainable healthcare. To ensure that the new HTA scheme 
provides affordability, access and cost saving and  maximum value for every rupee, the 
Committee, therefore, recommends mandatory provisions of i) time-bound integration 
of every HTA recommendation into appropriate national health programmes and 
essential medicine/device lists within 6 months, (ii) periodic capacity-building for 
officials and procurement officers (iii)  introduction of a performance-linked funding 
mechanism tied to number of HTA studies translated into policy within 12 months. 
According to the Committee, scientific evaluation of drugs, devices and treatment 
protocols should be the guide for health policy decisions to ensure optimal utilization of 
public resources. 
 
2.6.14 The Committee desires that more Research Hubs & Centres be established 
under the new HTA Scheme, particularly in unserved /underserved regions such as 
Jammu & Kashmir, Ladakh, the North-Eastern Region (NER) and in the Islands. 
These States/UTshave region-specific health challenges like, high-altitude diseases, 
tribal health issues, difficult terrain, which are poorly represented in current HTA 
studies. At present, HTAIn operates with only 8 Regional Hubs and 20 Resource 
Centres, the majority concentrated in southern states. Now, the proposal is to establish 
another 50 centres/hubs.The Committee observes that establishment of physical hubs is 
just an initial step. Without appropriate infrastructure and trained manpower, 
evidence generation for underserved areas is not possible. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that each proposed new centres/hubs should have a core team of HTA 
professionals including epidemiologists, health economists, and clinicians. Also, these 
remote hubs will need sustained annual recurring expenditure for manpower, training, 
data systems, etc. Hence, the Committee strongly recommends that these facts are 
appropriately taken care of in the new schema of HTA.

ABHIM during 15th FC period will be supported through VRDL scheme during 16th FC 
period. 
3.2.5 For 2026–27, the Department informed that it had initially proposed a substantially 
higher Budget Estimate (BE) of over ₹180 crore, taking into account the expanded scope and 
scale of activities envisaged under the VRDL and Infectious Diseases Research & Diagnostic 
Laboratories (IRDL) networks. This expansion proposes inclusion of new components such 
as enhanced surveillance activities, support to IRDLs, NABL accreditation and External 
Quality Assessment (EQA), and contingency support for outbreak management. Many of 
these activities were earlier supported under the scheme “Development of Tools / Support to 
Prevent Outbreaks & Epidemics,” with its core components being integrated into the VRDL 
Scheme to ensure continuity and optimal utilisation of resources. 

45 
 
3.2.6 However, against this proposal, the BE for 2026–27 has been fixed at ₹70.00 crore, as 
the proposal for expansion of the Scheme is currently under examination by the Expenditure 
Finance Committee. The approved BE thus reflects a calibrated and conservative allocation 
aimed at sustaining essential ongoing activities with zero growth and no improvements. Any 
further enhancement in allocation, including to address emerging public health threats such 
as new viral strains, outbreaks, or national health emergencies requiring expanded laboratory 
capacity, will be considered after completion of the EFC appraisal and receipt of requisite 
approvals 
3.2.7 The Committee sought to understand the reason for no capital expenditure being 
earmarked for the Head considering that the Head is for setting up of a nationwide network 
of laboratories for managing epidemics and national calamities. In reply, the Committee has 
been informed that capital expenditure is proposed and released under the Scheme only when 
new VRDLs are sanctioned, covering infrastructure development and procurement of 
essential laboratory equipment. Thereafter, the Scheme provides recurring support for 
operational expenses of these laboratories. Further, during the 15th Finance Commission 
period, VRDLs that have completed five years of recurring support under the DHR Scheme 
are being transitioned to the PM–Ayushman Bharat Health Infrastructure Mission (PM-
ABHIM) for long-term sustainability. Accordingly, 48 VRDLs are presently being supported 
under PM-ABHIM.Further, for the 16th Finance Commission period, it is proposed in the 
EFC that the recurring expenditure of IRDLs established under PM-ABHIM will be 
supported through the VRDL Scheme to ensure continuity and optimal utilization of the 
national laboratory network. 
 
3.2.8 The Committee has been given to understand that the 22.3% increase of BE 
2026-2027 at ₹70.00 crore over 2025-2026 BE of the scheme has been earmarked taking 
into consideration that the scheme of “Development of Tools / Support to Prevent 
Outbreaks & Epidemics,” is proposed to be discontinued from the 16thExpenditure 
Finance Cycle and its core components are to be integrated into the VRDL Scheme. 
Also, certain numbers of VRDLs are to be upgraded to IRDLs by including new 
components such as enhanced surveillance activities, support to IRDLs, NABL 
accreditation and External Quality Assessment (EQA), and contingency support for 
outbreak management. The funding pattern of the scheme suggests that the allocation 
over the past three years have been stagnant, but the utilization has been 100%. There 
has been a moderate increase of BE 2026-2027 at ₹70.00 crore against the projected 
demand of ₹180.00 crore thereby the percentage of variation of BE 2026-27 as 
compared to projected demand is 61.11 %. The Committee is of the opinion that it is 
disappointing, especially considering the significance of the scheme and some vital 
components are being merged with the scheme. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that with added responsibilities and structure of the scheme, the 
Department should make efforts to secure appropriate fund allocation under the 16th 
Finance Commission (2026-31) emphasizing the importance of investment in virology 
labs, genome surveillance and diagnostics to strengthen preparedness against future 
epidemics. 
 
 

46 
 
3.2.9 The Committee, further, observes the fact that capital expenditure is ‘nil’ under 
the scheme because capex is proposed and released under the Scheme only when new 
VRDLs are sanctioned. During the 15th Finance Commission period, VRDLs that have 
completed five years of recurring support under the DHR Scheme and for the 16th 
Finance Commission period, it is proposed in the Expenditure Finance Committee that 
the recurring expenditure of IRDLs established under PM-ABHIM will be supported 
through the VRDL Scheme to ensure continuity and optimal utilization of the national 
laboratory network. Accordingly, DHR apprised the Committee that no proposals are 
there in the pipeline for new labs under the scheme. The Committee observes that the 
map of VRDL labs shows gaps in the geographical spread of State level and regional 
level labs. India is a country with more than a billion population, extreme topographic 
and climatic diversity accompanied by rising zoonotic and climate-amplified threats 
like, Nipah, Dengue surges, Avian influenza, etc which require that the gaps of regional 
and State level labs across the country should be abridged. Accordingly, the Committee 
recommends that VRDLs should be upgraded to IRDLs and these factors may be given 
due consideration and even upgradation across the country should be undertaken. 
 
3.2.10 The Committee takes note of the achievements of VRDL scheme like Integrating 
of VRDLN portal with Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP) which has 
enhanced the public health surveillance and the launching of the Quarterly VRDL 
Bulletin at the National VRDL Conclave 2025 has provided a transparent platform for 
real-time data on viral infection trends. The Committee is of the view that the viral data 
base of VRDLs must serve as systematic sentinel surveillance platform in India for 
early detection of emerging/ re-emerging infectious diseases in the ensuing year, 
keeping into consideration the veiled threat of high risk pathogens viz., MPoX, Nipah, 
Zika, CCHF, Avian influenza etc.The Committee observes that such steps would ensure 
early-warning and containment of outbreaks.

i. Multi-Disciplinary Research Units (MRUs) 
3.3.9 Originally conceptualized during the 12th Plan Period (2012–17) under the umbrella 
scheme Development of Infrastructure for Promotion of Health Research, the MRU initiative 
aims to bridge longstanding gaps in research capacity, laboratory infrastructure, and 
scientific output across medical institutions in India. Following successful implementation 
during previous plan periods—including an interim extension aligned with the 14th Finance 
Commission, the continuation of the scheme for the 15th Finance Commission cycle (2021–
22 to 2025–26) was approved. As of now, 123 MRUs including 5 MRUs in Private Medical 
Colleges have been established across various States and Union Territories. These units 
primarily focus on Non-Communicable Diseases (NCDs), while also addressing emerging 
public health challenges through clinical trials, multi-centre research, and capacity-building 
initiatives. The key objectives of MRUs are:- 
i. To strengthen the research environment within medical colleges by establishing 
dedicated, state-of-the-art MRUs. 
ii. To bridge infrastructural gaps that hinder the conduct of quality health research by 
creating well-equipped research facilities. 
iii. To build research capacity and human resources in the field of health research 
through training, mentorship, and hands-on project involvement. 
iv. To ensure equitable geographical distribution of health research infrastructure by 
establishing MRUs across underserved and underrepresented regions. 
v. To contribute to improved public health outcomes through the generation of 
evidence-based diagnostic methods, processes, and scientific knowledge. 
vi. To undertake clinical trials in accordance with the Allocation of Business Rules of the 
Government of India. 
vii To promote multi-centric research projects involving MRUs, medical colleges, and 
research institutions for addressing national and regional health priorities. 
3.3.10 Monitoring of MRUs is carried out at both the institutional and central level to ensure 
effective functioning, accountability, and alignment with the objectives of the sub-scheme. 
The Local Research Advisory Committee (LRAC)considers and approves research proposals. 
The Executive Committee ensures broad participation of all Departments in submitting 
research proposals to the MRU. At the central level, DHR administers and monitors the 
progress of MRUs through a structured framework, supported by the Programme Monitoring 
and Implementation Unit (PMIU) comprising of Project Manager, Finance Manager, 
Scientists, and other support staff.

3.5.4 The relatively low expenditure in the initial years of the Scheme was primarily due to 
the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic and foreign training programmes were suspended 
during this period. Medical colleges, being part of the frontline healthcare system, were 
extensively involved in Covid-19 management, which further contributed to the reduced 
activity under the Scheme during the pandemic years.. The reasons for the sudden increase 
observed in FY 2024-25 is due to the integration of ICMR’s capacity building programmes 
into the DHR–HRD scheme in January 2024. Prior to this integration, ICMR was operating 
its international fellowship programmes separately. After integration, a total of 65 
international fellowships were recorded, reflecting the consolidated numbers from both 
schemes.  
 
3.5.5 DHR has informed that the Guidelines of HRD schemes have been amended and 
scope of inclusion has been broadened in case of Startup Grant for Induction into Biomedical 
Research Scheme. Broadening of the scope of the Start Up grant has increased the number of 
applications and beneficiaries from biomedical and health researchers. While the applications 
granted support in the year 2024-25 were only 10, there was a quantum leap to 57 in the year 
2025-26 (approx. 5 times). There was a corresponding increase in the number of 
beneficiaries from the non- metro cities with 40% in year 2024- 25; to 71% in 2025-26. The 
awardees from Medical colleges also increased from 2 in the year 2024-25 to 8 in the year 
2025-26. 
 
3.2.6 Further, the Department has conducted a third-party evaluation through the National 
Productivity Council in the Financial Year 2025–26 to assess the reasons for poor proposal 
quality and low participation from young faculty and researchers in medical colleges. 
 
Major Key Findings: 
(i) Limited Awareness and Outreach: Many young faculty members were not 
adequately aware of the schemes and opportunities available under DHR; 
(ii) Capacity Constraints: Lack of structured mentorship and limited exposure to 
proposal writing and project management skills resulted in weak technical quality 
of submissions; and 
(iii) Time Constraints: Heavy teaching and clinical responsibilities left limited time for 
young faculty to engage in research activities.  
 
Follow-up Actions Initiated: 
(i) Enhanced Awareness Campaigns: Wider dissemination of scheme details through 
workshops, webinars, and social media outreach to enhance the participation; 
(ii) Capacity Building: Training programmes on proposal writing, research 
methodology, and project management targeted at young faculty and early-career 
researchers; 
(iii) Streamlined Processes: Increasing the frequency of Technical Evaluation 
Committee (TEC) meetings and simplifying application procedures to reduce 
delays; and

and helping young faculties in developing competitive proposals.

3.5.8 DHR through its Fellowships abroad programme under HRD scheme supports 
advanced trainings of Indian scientists and researchers in foreign countries, with condition 
that they serve back in India utilizing the skills gained. To counter the challenge of “brain 
drain” and to retain skilled researchers in India, the DHR, has undertaken several specific 
initiatives aimed at providing better facilities and competitive career prospects comparable to 
international standards. The key initiatives include: 
 
(i) NRI/PIO/OCI Research Support Programme: This programme has been launched to 
encourage Indian-origin scientists working abroad to return and contribute to 
biomedical and health research in India. It provides contractual research positions and 
financial assistance, thereby leveraging the expertise of highly trained professionals 
with exposure to advanced technologies and methodologies. 
 
(ii) Training Fellowships: Researchers are supported through various training workshops 
and travel grants programmes for international exposure, enabling them to strengthen 
their skills and contribute effectively to national research priorities. 
 
(iii) Foreign Training and Repatriation Support: Faculties and researchers are facilitated 
for foreign training opportunities and are supported upon their return to India, 
ensuring knowledge transfer and capacity building.

3.5.24 The Committee thereafter wanted to be updated on the status of Anti-cancer vaccine. 
In response ICMR submitted that the interest in the development of cancer is ever growing 
from a public health perspective. Efforts and scientific progress are being made globally in 
this field. At present, the availability of personalized mRNA-based vaccines for specific 
cancers and its clinical use will depend on the completion of ongoing trials and subsequent 
regulatory approvals. A generalised or universal “anti‑cancer vaccine” is unlikely to be 
introduced for public use in the coming year. It is important to distinguish these emerging 
therapeutic vaccines from preventive anti‑cancer vaccines, which are already established and 
in public health use. In this domain, the Government of India has taken a significant step 
through the planned national HPV vaccination campaign, which directly contributes to 
cancer prevention. The Government on 28 February 2026, has launched the HPV vaccination 
programme wherein all 14‑year‑old girls across the country will be offered a single dose of 
the HPV vaccine through government health facilities. This national initiative aims to 
substantially reduce the future burden of cervical cancer.

3.5.26 On the Uniform Cancer Treatment Protocol, the Committee acquiesce with the 
submission of ICMR, being the field experts, that it does not recommend “uniform 
cancer treatment protocol”. Having said that the Committee observes that the 
treatment procedures and cost involved in a particular type of cancer in the country 
have wide gaps between a government institution and a private institution. While the 
Committee acknowledges that DHR does not have any say in the cost involved in 
treatment procedures, the Committee recommends the ICMR’s National Cancer 
Registry Programme (NCRP) along with the D/o H&FW should undertake a study to 
identify a way to address the issue of wide gaps in treatment procedures for a particular 
type of cancer between a government institution and a private institution. The 
Committee, however, is of the considered view that as a beginning, DHR should 
formulate treatment protocol for common cancers like oral, cervical and breast cancers 
and come up with a broad based for its treatment procedures and guidelines. Like the 
submission of ICMR, since National Institute of Cancer Prevention & research 
(NICPR)‑ICMR updates are directly linked to national clinical guidelines, the 
Committee perceives such a study would help to lessen the gaps. 
 
3.5.27 Regarding anti-cancer vaccine, the Committee has been impressed upon that 
efforts and scientific progress is being made in this field globally. The availability of 
personalized mRNA-based vaccines for specific cancers and its clinical use depends on 
the completion of ongoing trials and subsequent regulatory framework. The only anti-
cancer vaccination as of now available, both globally as well as in India, is the HPV 
vaccine. The Committee hopes that India, through ICMR, enters this field as the rising 
incidence of cancer among the population, especially among the youth, in recent times is 
alarmingly high. Accordingly, the Committee recommends ICMR should make efforts 
to make itself a part of on-going anti- cancer vaccination research projects globally in 
coordination with international entities like WHO and come forward for regulatory 
approval for clinical use.

3.6.4 The Committee asked the Department to comment on the total allocation of funds 
under the Scheme in 2026-2027 &2025-2026 at₹351.06 crore and ₹350.49 crore, 
respectively, being stagnant as compared to a hike from 2024-2025 at₹ 212.21 crore. Also, 
whether the funding at ₹351.06 crore in 2026-2027 is sufficient for multi- sectoral and 
national platforms, given the interdisciplinary nature of One Health and Bio- security.  
 
3.6.5 As reply, DHR stated that the allocation for 2025–26 (₹350.49 crore) and 2026–27 
(₹351.06 crore) has remained broadly stable as the scheme is presently in a consolidation and 
transition phase. The objectives under the earlier plan period have largely been completed, 
and current expenditures are primarily directed towards committed liabilities and milestone-
based disbursements of projects already approved under the existing EFC/SFC framework. In 
2025–26, 207 ongoing research projects across thematic areas are being supported, and 
projects sanctioned in 2024–25 and 2025–26 are being implemented within the previously 
approved financial envelope; hence, annual allocations have not increased incrementally at 
this stage.Further, multi-sectoral/national platform components are being sequenced, with 
initial outlay kept conservative while foundational governance, interoperability, and 
institutional coordination are established. The requirement will be reviewed during the RE 
exercise, and allocations for 2026–27 may be re-assessed based on implementation progress 
and utilization trends. 
 
3.6.6 Regarding adequacy, DHR opined that ₹351.06 crore 2026-27 may be sufficient for 
sustaining ongoing projects and initiating incremental platform strengthening. However, 
given the interdisciplinary and cross-sectoral nature of One Health and bio-security, full-
scale national platforming and rapid expansion may require additional, phased investments 
and convergence with allied sectoral programs. Accordingly, funding needs will be reviewed 
at RE stage in line with the pace of platform roll-out and readiness of implementing entities

CHAPTER – IV  
INDIAN COUNCIL OF MEDICAL RESEARCH (ICMR) 
 
4.1 The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), headquartered in New Delhi, is 
India's apex organization for formulating, coordinating, and promoting biomedical research. 
As one of the world's oldest medical research institutions, ICMR operates under the 
Department of Health Research (DHR) within the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 
Government of India. Its research agenda aligns closely with national health priorities, 
focusing on communicable diseases, fertility control, maternal and child health, nutritional 
disorders, environmental and occupational health issues, and non-communicable diseases 
such as cancer, cardiovascular conditions, diabetes, blindness, and mental health disorders. 
 
4.2 The Secretary, DHR in his oral evidence related to the examination of Demand 2026-
27of DHR submitted that in BE 2026-27, the Department has got a budgetary allocation from 
the Government of Rs.4,821 crore. Out of which, on the allocation of Rs.4,000 crores for 
ICMR, he stated that this does not include any money from revenue or from any other source 
from within the ICMR.  This is the funding from the Government to the ICMR 
 
4.3 While explaining the ICMR budgetary system, the Secretary submitted that major 
portion is Grants-in-Aid General which is basically the money spent on research i.e. research 
projects and research institutions. The remaining amount is for the salary of ICMR scientists, 
technical staff and administrative staff, capital assets, etc.  He also informed that ICMR 
pensions are not paid out of salaries head but out of the Grants-in-Aid General. Under the 
research budget, there is intramural research, which means research in ICMR institutions, 
and there is extramural research, where ICMR funds more than 300 institutions in the 
country to do research.  
 
4.4 The Committee was also informed by the Secretary, DHR that ICMR was an inward-
looking organization in the past, but now it has adapted itself to be an outward looking 
organization. ICMR are now spending majority of their funds on extramural grants, which 
means that all the other medical and research institutions in the country are funded through 
ICMR.  According to the Secretary, DHR who is also DG, ICMR, that is a very substantial 
change. Further, before 2023, ICMR was doing largely descriptive research. After that there 
has been very substantial reduction in money being spent on descriptive research. As of now, 
ICMR is spending close to 40 per cent for development research that is, actual development 
of new technologies and their clinical evaluation.

out of the Grants-in-Aid General which is basically the amount of money reflected to be 
spent on research i.e. research projects and research institutions. The Committee finds 
that the objective of Grants-in-Aid Scheme is to provide fundfor research projects. 
While Grants-in-Aid General Head cover funding for other items alongwith research 
project. The Committee seeks the Department to submit a clarification in the matter.

4.7.8 As part the examination of budgetary allocation of ICMR for 2026-27, the Committee 
sought a comparison of ICMR corresponding with research institutes of Developed countries 
on public funding of health research. The details so furnished by ICMR are that the

Medical Research Council $12.33 billion (0.36% of GDP), and Australia’s National Health

Department of Health Research (DHR) receives about$385 million annually, 0.01% of GDP.

Performance Evaluation Committee’s prominent recommendations pertaining to its 
comparative study include- 
 
1. To improve research quality and impact, implement a peer review and monitoring 
system integrating constructive feedback, modelled on the NIH (National 
Institutes of Health), USA. 
2.  ICMR/DHR should enhance its presence, visibility and influence in the WHO 
system. Apart from continuous engagement, active participation at the World 
Health Assembly is of paramount importance to showcase India’s health research. 
3. ICMR should actively participate in other major global health forums, foster 
leadership roles in international research consortia, and increase representation in 
global policy and advisory bodies. 
 
4.7.9 The Committee notes that Performance Evaluation Committees of ICMR are 
formed every 5 years and the last committee was constituted in 2022. Its report reflects 
0.01% of GDP as Government’s spending on Health Research in India, But, on the

Government spends 0.02% of GDP for Health Research vis-a vis U.S. National 
Institutes of Health receives about $47.77 billion annually (0.17% of GDP), the UK

Medical Research Council $12.33 billion (0.36% of GDP), and Australia’s National 
Health and Medical Research Council $1.34 billion (0.07% of GDP). The percentage of 
the Government’s spending on Health Research in India has been stagnant for the last 
5 years. Nevertheless, the statistics is disappointing. The Government is doing a lot of 
things in its attempt to make India a developed country. Viskit Bharat@47, which is a 
part of this attempt, is a revolutionary thought and to achieve that the nation need a 
young population as well as a healthy population. The Committee therefore 
recommends for higher budgetary support to DHR as percentage of GDP as 
comparable to leading Asian economies such as China, South Korea, Japan, etc. Efforts 
to be made to choke out a road map to bridge the research and investment gap by 
extracting measurable outcome from intramural and extramural project, especially in 
terms of publications, patents and clinical guidelines. The Committee further 
recommends for adequate budgetary support towards theoretic development advanced 
trails and indigenous innovations. Action plans should be chalked out for PPP based 
funding on mission mode to reduce long term dependency on expensive imported 
therapies.  
4.7.10 Every health scheme/program/research/study should be conceived as a step 
towards creating a healthy population who would directly/indirectly contribute to the 
GDP of the country. The Committee feels that at 0.02% of its GDP, India is at a very 
lower position compared to developed countries in the field of Health Research 
expenditure. As of now, India’s representation and contribution to the global health 
forums is not much remarkable. The Committee feels that India has no dearth of 
talents. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the Department to timely fulfil their 
commitments towards the on-going projects, which would in turn help them secure

allowed to retain the revenues generated by ICMR rather than depositing all of it to the

4.7.11 Further, the Committee endorses the suggestions of the Performance Evaluation

trials, etc. Hence, the Committee recommends further strengthening of the role of DHR 
as a regulatory entity through frequent trainings for Ethics Committees members and 
participants, introduction of digital tools for monitoring and timely review of 
guidelines. ICMR should ensure that participation in clinical trials is based on genuine 
informed consent and all measures to ensure this shall be taken by DHR. 
 
4.10  Contemporary and Critical Areas of Research in India 
 
4.10.1 When the Committee enquired about the measures taken by ICMR to translate its 
expanding NCD research portfolio into public health interventions, viz. including its research 
outcomes with national initiatives on National Programme for Prevention and Control of 
Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS), etc. DHR furnished the 
following domain wise details: - 
 

92 
 
a) Oncology

for oral suspension (PFOS) of 6-mercaptopurine (PREVALL), which helps in 
accurate dosing for children undergoing treatment for Acute Lymphoblastic 
Leukaemia (ALL).  
 
(ii) ICMR’s CARE-Clinical Pharmacology initiative focuses on therapeutic 
monitoring of anti-cancer drugs like sunitinib and docetaxel, which demonstrates 
that drug monitoring improves patients' quality of life (QOL) and reduces 
treatment costs.

cancers in Cachar, Assam demonstrated the effectiveness of frontline health

factors associated with IGBC and other premalignant conditions (chronic 
cholecystitis, hyperplasia, metaplasia, dysplasia, carcinoma in situ) so that an

(v) The pattern of care and survival studies (POCSS) provided information on 
improved care strategies and early detection measures. 
(vi) ICMR conducted multicentric studies on breast cancer that demonstrated that 
pesticide exposure, benign breast diseases, family history of breast cancers, family 
history of other cancers, age at menopause, and physical activity are considered 
important risk factors.  
 
(vii) ICMR evaluated the efficacy of multiple point-of-care systems for detection of oral 
potentially malignant disorders (OPMDs) and to develop a prognostic model 
combining clinical/ auto-fluorescence images, saliva markers, cytology, histology,

criteria for positivity of Epstein B Virus (EBV).

(i) The Centre for Advanced Research (CAR) for cardiovascular disease (St. John’s,

where Non-Physician Health Workers (NPHWs) are trained to deliver protocol-
based care.  

93 
 
 
(ii) India Hypertension Control Initiative (IHCI) in private sector: ICMR initiated

(i) ICMR’ Young Diabetes Registry is the largest national registry for youth onset

ICMR established a population-based stroke registry at Dibrugarh and 
observed that stroke incidence rate was 160 /100000 population in this region. An 
unusually higher rates of haemorrhagic stroke (65-70%) were observed in the stroke 
patients in this population. In view of this, ICMR with support from the Govt. of 
Assam, had initiated a research project to establish a clinical stroke care pathway for 
management of acute stroke cases at Dibrugarh and Tezpur. MSU (Mobile Stroke 
Unit) can play a crucial role at the sub-district (block or CHC) level, especially in

leading cause of death.

and international collaborations focused on dementia prevention and elder care. 
(i) SMRUTHI (cmRCT) cohort: 3,000 at‑risk elders via MRHRUs in Tripura,
