Recommendations/Observations 
 
14.8       The Committee is surprised to note  that our premier Institute in the field of 
medical research has been working with th e minimum staff for all these years. The 
very fact that not a single post has been  created during the last 25 years confirms 
Committee’s concerns in this regard. Not only this, a large number of  posts, that too, 
in scientific and technical grade are lying vacant. The Committee is not aware since 
when such a situation has been continuing . The Committee can imagine the kind of 
work stress being faced by our scientists, specially during the time of epidemic 
outbreaks. The Committee recommends that al l the existing vacant posts in ICMR 

should be filled up without any further delay. All 500 posts of scientists and 1000 
matching posts of research fellows and technical posts should be created at the earliest 
and filled up. This exercise needs to be c arried out in a time-bound manner. It should 
be ensured that unduly long time is not taken in getting the posts created, followed by 
a protracted exercise of getting them filled up. Similarly, concerted efforts would also 
be required for creation and filling up of 210 posts of scientists and 400 posts of 
technical staff required for the Department  of Health Research. The Department will 
have to play a proactive role so that lack of specialized manpower does not hamper 
the crucial research activities, both ongoing and proposed. 
 
Action Taken 
  
 Needs no comments. 
 
Comments of the Committee 
 
 The Committee had invested the creation of posts of scientists and matching 
posts of research fellows and technical po sts with Parliamentary support and it was 
the obligation of the Department to make earnest efforts to apprise the authorities 
concerned of the Committee’s recommendation in this regard so that necessary 
action could be initiated towards creating and filling up the posts.

the impression that it does not attach much  importance to the creation of necessary

matter with an astute sense of sincerity and urgency.

III .  ROLE OF NGOs 
Recommendations/Observations   
 
3.3 The Committee apprehends that the di scontinued/blacklisted NGOs may also 
resurface again by changing their name or place of work. The Committee would like 

to be apprised about the specific steps ta ken by the Department to thwart any such 
attempts by such NGOs and share with it su ch instances, if any, when it has been 
successful in preventing re-entry of such NGOs in the NACO network. 
 
Action Taken 
 
It may be mentioned that NGOs which do not optimally perform are 
discontinued but can be included in a proce ss for selection and th e verifying that all 
the drawbacks have been removed or not. However, if an NGO has been terminated 
on any financial misappropriation then it will not be allowed to be part of above 
process. To ensure that, all the SACS will k eep the list of NGOs terminated because of 
financial misappropriations and their reques t will not be considered. To ensure that 
such organizations will not resurface ag ain by changing the name, SACS has a 
transparent NGO selection process which includes the following steps:  
• Issue of Expression of interest th rough open advertisement in all leading                 
newspapers.   
• Preliminary screening of applications by the Technical Advisory Committee (TAC) 
for Joint Appraisal Team (JAT) visit. 
• Field visit by JAT teams to assess institutional capability and program effectiveness 
of the screened NGOs. The JAT will be comp rised of external consultants / experts 
both for programme and finance and SACS officials. Specific assessment tool has 
been developed for the field level assessment and minimum mark has been fixed 
for qualification for short listing for final selection. JAT will assess the NGO based 
on specific check list developed by NACO which includes, governance system, 
staffing and organizational structure and capacity, finance management system in 

the organization, experience of organizatio n in health sector specifically in HIV 
/AIDS programme, planning, monitoring and supervision system in the NGO etc.. 
During the interaction with office bearers  of NGOs, chances of  resurface again by 
changing the name of NGO will be ruled out. 
• Finalize NGOs partners by TAC headed  by Project director of the SAC. 
Empanelled NGO list to be approved by the executive committee of the 
respective SAC to initiate the project implementation. 
• Contracting of NGOs approved by the executive committee. 
• Development of project proposal an d assessment of the same through 
conducting workshop. 
• Contract period of TI implementation is 2 years. 
The above mentioned processes also involv e visiting the NGOs and verifying the 
credentials onsite.

Recommendations/Observations  
 
11.6 The Committee notes that the Link Worker Scheme is an intensive rural-based 
intervention reaching out to the marginal ized groups which remain uncovered even 
after the expansion of urban based prev ention programme. However, the Committee 
notes that the same is being implemented on ly in 18 States as of now. The Committee 

recommends to the Department to assess the need to cover the re maining States and 
closely monitor the scheme as  the success of this scheme is crucial for achieving the 
goal of halting and reversing the epidemic of AIDS. 
 
Action Taken 
 
The Link Worker Scheme was devised to  provide HIV related rural outreach 
services to HRG & Vulnerable population, in the identified priority districts (Based on 
HIV Sentinel Surveillance) of the coun try. Accordingly, the scheme is being 
implemented with the focus of saturating the rural HRG and vulnerable population of 
the high prevalent states i.e. Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Manipur & 
Nagaland. Currently, the link worker scheme is also being implemented in the states 
with low prevalence rate e.g. UP, Bihar. In  FY 2010-11, two districts of state of Punjab 
will be covered under the scheme, whereas e xpansion of the scheme will take place to 
another 61 districts in the existi ng 18 states. In addition to this, proposal is also made 
for including 30 additional districts which are vulnerable due to high rate of migration 
to other regions.  
Under the Link Worker Scheme, close monitoring of the scheme is suggested as one of 
the key deliverables of the lead NGO wh ich are responsible for managing and 
identification of the district level NGOs. Th e monitoring indicators of the scheme are 
already developed and based on these indica tors monthly reports are received from 
all the districts.  For addressing the gaps  identified during monthly reports and for 
supportive supervision, regular field visits  are made by the LWS representatives at 
NACO & SACS.

II. BUDGETARY PROVISIONS 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
2.4 The Committee appreciates that with fo cused intervention of NACO there is a 
considerable decline in unspent balances available with the societies. The Committee 
would, however, like to point out that availability of unspent balance with some 
SACS, like Karnataka SACS (Rs. 11.34 crore), Tamil Nadu (Rs. 8.40 crore) and West 
Bengal (Rs. 8.99 crore) is still quite high. The Committee, therefore, recommends to the 
Department to introduce stricter monitori ng mechanism and financial discipline so 
that funds do not get accumulated and remain unutilized. 
 
Action Taken  
 
Recommendations of the Committee are no ted for guidance. It is always the 
endeavor of the Government to keep bala nces with the SACS to the minimum. The 
final availability of unspent balances at the end of the financial year 2009-10 for the 
SACS are Karnataka (Rs.9.65 crore), Tam il Nadu (Rs.7.06crore) and West Bengal 
(Rs.7.06 crore). The financial monitoring/d iscipline is being watched through 
Computerized Project Finance Management System (CPFMS). However, there is a 
necessity to have funds available with SACS at the beginning of the financial year as 
working capital requirement to meet the committed liabilities of salary, operational 
expenses etc. in the beginning of the year as first installment is released only in 
May/June. 
 

 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Department enabling it to bring 
down the availability of unspent balances  with the various SACS at the end of the 
financial year 2009-10, like Karnataka (from Rs. 11.34 crore to Rs.9.65 crore), Tamil 
Nadu (from Rs. 8.40 crore to Rs.7.06 crore) a nd West Bengal (from Rs. 8.99 crore  to 
Rs.7.06 crore). However, the same is still on  the higher side and is not justifiable. 
The Committee takes note of the requireme nts of working capital funds with SACS 
at the beginning of the financial year to meet the committed liabilities like salary, 
operational expenses etc. as first installmen t of funds is released only in May/June.  
At the same time, it is also a fact that releases to Stat es are being done through e-
transfer to reduce transit delay with salary payments to the employees of the 
peripheral units in many States being made  electronically. In such a scenario, it 
cannot be considered appropriate and justifiabl e that funds to the tune of  Rs 7 to 8 
crores are available as unspent balance at the beginning of the year which could 
have been utilized by the SACS for th eir targeted activities. The Committee, 
accordingly, recommends that all activities as included in the Annual Action Plan 
issued to the States before the close of the previous year and placed on the NACO 
website need to be implemented as envisaged.

NACO has issued detailed Operational Gu ideline for selection and contracting

served to all NGOs/CBOs during contract with SACS. (The contractual norms are 
attached as Annexure II)  
 
The Operational Guideline for Targeted Intervention Part – 1 under NACP III 
clearly details the process of selectio n of NGOs/CBOs to implement targeted 
intervention projects. It is a transparent process having following steps: 
• Issue of Expression of interest through open advertisement in all leading news 
papers.  
• Preliminary screening of applications by the Technical Advisory Committee 
(TAC) for Joint Appraisal Team (JAT) visit.  
• Field visit by JAT teams to assess institutional capability and program 
effectiveness of the screened NGOs. Th e JAT will be comprised of external 
consultants / experts both for programme and finance and SACS officials. 
Specific assessment tool has been develo ped for the field level assessment and 
minimum mark has been fixed for qua lification for short listing for final 
selection. JAT will assess the NGO based on specific check list developed by 
NACO which includes, governance system , staffing and organizational structure 
and capacity, finance management system in the organization, experience of 

organization in health sector specific ally in HIV /AIDS programme, planning 
monitoring and supervision system in the NGO etc.. 
• Finalize NGOs partners by TAC headed  by Project director of the SAC. 
Empanelled NGO list to be approved by the executive committee of the 
respective SAC to initiate the project implementation. 
• Contracting of NGOs approved by the executive committee. 
• Development of project proposal an d assessment of the same through 
conducting workshop. 
 
Project Directors of State AIDS Control Societies are responsible for monitoring, 
taking up decisions on selection of NGOs based on the recommendation of executive 
committee at state level. The delay of reco very of unspent amount is subjected to

appointed by State AIDS Control Societies, delay or non response from discontinued

NGOs which indulge in fraud and fina ncial embezzlement are subjected to 
strict action with legal advice. SACS w ill not consider these organizations for any 
future programme.

Besides that, out of 27 States/ UTs, no rec overy has been made so far in case of 
Assam, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, 
Meghalaya, Nagaland, Orissa, Punjab and UP. All these States have varying 
number of discontinued NGOs with Ma dhya Pradesh having the maximum 
number of 23 NGOs showing recovery of Rs. 60,53,234. What is a cause of serious 
concern for the Committee is that in most of the cases, NGOs are simply not 
traceable. It seems that corrective measures  like monitoring mechanism in force at 
NACO and respective SACS level, State visits of NACO Officers, six monthly 
financial audit by external auditors have either not proved to be effective enough 
or are not being implemented properly. Th e Committee would appreciate if all the 
cases of discontinued NGOs are pursued vigorously and required action taken 
without any further delay. 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
3.5 The Committee is constrained to obse rve that the achievement level under 
many of the physical target s set during 2009-10 has been far from satisfactory. There 
are instances of severe under-achievements  under the components  like –Setting new 
core group targeted interventions; setti ng up new bridge population targeted 

interventions; setting up new Blood Comp onent Separation Units; setting up new 
District Level Blood Banks etc. The Committee fails to understand that under such 
circumstances how the Department has utiliz ed more than 98% of the funds during 
2009-10 without achieving the satisfactory le vel of achievements under many of the 
physical targets. The Department needs to understand that it is good to achieve 
financial targets but what is more import ant is that achievement of the financial 
targets should be commensurate with the achi evement of the set physical targets. The 
same is apparently missing here. Under such circumstances,  the Committee has 
serious doubts over the planning and the su bsequent execution strategies of most of 
the components of the programme. The Committee can only infer that either the funds 
sought have been miscalculated or the Department has pumped in more money under 
certain components running successfully wher eby it could show a higher percentage 
of Utilization of allocated funds. The Department needs to clarify the same. 
Action Taken 
The total target set for NACP III (2007- 2012) is 2100, average 420 TI projects 
should on board every year. Out of which th e number of TI projects as of now are 
1568, in three years’ period. It is well above th e target for three years. It may be noted 
that the number of TIs is estimated an d designed based on High Risk Groups’ 
mapping that is undertaken to find out the High Risk Group population across the 
country. Number of interventions projects for each State is calculated based on the 
size estimation mentioned above to ensure the saturation of coverage of High Risk 
Population. 
 
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 

  
  The Committee had put up a simple query to the Department as to how the 
utilization of funds, which is almost 100 per cent, is not commensurate with the 
achievement of the physical targets, which are on the lower side in respect of several 
important components of the Programme. The response of the Department in no 
way addresses the issues raised by the Committee. In the absence of any 
justification, the Committee, as it said ear lier, can only infer that some serious 
problem areas in planning and the subsequent execution strategies of most of the 
components of the Programme exist. The De partment needs to take up this aspect 
very seriously. 
IV  SETTING UP OF NEW BLOOD COMPONENT SEPARATION UNITS 
(BCSUs) 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
 
4.2 The Committee is constrained to observ e that the data made available to the 
Committee through the response to a query made twice reveals that the Department 
has fixed a target of 162 for setting up of new Blood Component Separation Units by 
the end of the Eleventh Plan . The Committee notes that no  target was fixed for the 
first year, i.e., 2007 – 08, and for 2008 – 09 an d 2009 – 10, 40 BCSUs each were kept as 
targets. However, a cumulative achievemen t of only 47 BCSUs could be made till 
February 2010. Out of the total target of 162 un its for the Eleventh Plan period, a total 
of 115 more such units are required to be set up during the last two years of the 
Eleventh Plan period. The Committee would like the same to be clarified. 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
 
It is submitted that under Phase – III of National AIDS Control Programme, the 
target for setting up of 80 Blood Componen t Separation Units was fixed. As per the 

procurement cycle, the procurement of equipm ents for these units was to be taken up 
during 2008 – 09 and 2009 – 10 for 40 set of equi pments during each year.  No target 
was fixed during the 1st year, in view of the regulatory requirement for physical 
infrastructure for setting up of BCSUs, wh ich entails 7 rooms with the total covered 
area of 150 sq. metres and necessary electrical and mechanical fittings. 
It is also submitted that even after the procurement of equipments, the process 
of obtaining a license from the Drugs Controlle r General (India) is at various stages of 
processing viz. preliminary inspection; joint inspection and final inspection etc. which 
was followed up with the concerned authorities at every stage. Because of this, out of 
the 80 such units, 49 units have obtained a license to operate and for the remaining 
units, the matter is being followed up. 
Thus, the target for setting up of BCSUs as reflected in the report as 162, is the 
cumulative target for NACP, Phase – III.  
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
 The Committee has been informed that under Phase III of NACO, against the 
target during 2007-08 to 2009-10 for setting up of 80 Blood Component Separation 
Units, 40 Units have obtained a license to  operate so far. The Committee is not 
aware whether the required infrastructure of 7 fully equipped rooms with total 
covered area of 150 sq. meters has been made available for these units. For the 
remaining 31 units, the process of procuring a license from the Drug Controller 
General of India is yet to be completed. Against this backdrop, the Committee is 
not very hopeful about the achievement level of 162 Blood Component Separation 

Units to be set up under Phase III of NA CO. The Committee can only emphasize 
that every conceivable effort needs to be made to accomplish this target. 
 
V.  SETTING UP OF NEW DISTRICT LEVEL BLOOD BANKS. 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
 
5.3 The Committee is dismayed at the fact that the Department has not been able to 
take up the matter of setting up of the di strict level blood banks with a sense of 
urgency. The Department itself is aware  that these 39 Blood Banks have been 
identified on the basis of an assessment of  urgent requirement in underserved areas. 
Hence, a delay in setting up of the blood ba nks as envisaged, is against Department’s 
obligations to see that the facilities reach these underserved areas. Most of the reasons 
cited for the delay are non-availability of  adequate infrastructure, manpower and 
delay in issuance of license. The Department needs to play a pro-active role by taking 
up the matter with the concerned State Gove rnments as well as the agencies at an 
appropriate level to expedite the procedural  formalities. The Department should also 
consider providing appropriate additional funds, if required, for infrastructure and 
manpower related matters so that there is no delay due to financial constraints. 
 
Action Taken 
 
It is submitted that the target of taki ng up blood banks in the 39 districts was 
identified during the planning of National AIDS Control Programme (NACP), Phase – 
III; wherein both National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) and concerned State 
Governments have specific roles. NACO was supposed to provide equipment and the 
annual recurring grant for one Lab Techni cian and consumables, while the State 
Government has to provide physical infrastr ucture in terms of building with a space 

of 100 sq. mts in 5(five) rooms; manpower  in terms of Medical Officer, Laboratory 
Technician, Nurse and support staff. As pe r the laid down scheme for modernization 
of blood banks, the funds for infrastructu re and manpower are not included in the 
Pattern of Assistance and is the responsibility of the State Government. 
 
NACO has already completed the procurement of equipments and the matter 
is followed up with concerned State Gove rnments, so that once the physical 
infrastructure in terms of building is ready, further action can be initiated. 
 
In view of this follow up, Blood Banks in 8 ou t of the 39 identified districts have come 
up now and for the remaining blood banks, continuous follow up is in process. 
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
 The Committee acknowledges the stand of the Department that the funds for 
infrastructure and manpower are not included in the Pattern of Assistance and is 
the responsibility of the State Governme nts. Factual position as given by the 
Department clearly indicates that majority  of the State Governments have failed to 
fulfil their commitment of providing physica l infrastructure, i.e. a building having 
an area of 100 sq.mts. and required manpower of Medical Officer, Lab Technician, 
Nurse and Support Staff. Moreover, when NACO has already procured the 
equipments for these Blood Banks, they  need to be supplemented by State 
Governments coming forward with fulfillment of their commitments. The 
Committee can only reiterate that the Depart ment has to play a pro-active role by 
taking up the matter with the concerned State Governments, if need be at the 
highest level. It can also help the States financially which are facing resource 

constraints. The Committee is of the firm op inion that the Department has to play 
the role of catalyst in achieving the targets under this component rather than 
remaining rigid on procedural aspects. 
  
Recommendations/Observations 
 
5.7 The Committee welcomes this new initiative  of the Department for establishing 
four Metro Blood Banks as Centres of Excellence. However, the Committee is 
unhappy to note that the slow progress of th e Department in realizing this initiative 
which has been pending since 2008 – 09. Th ese blood banks would not only act as 
model blood banks with latest equipments and technology but would also be of great 
help in meeting the ever rising dema nds of these metro cities. The Committee 
however notes that from the records available with it, that no dead lines have been set 
regarding making the same functional. Keep ing in mind the delay already made in 
implementation of this initiative, the Co mmittee recommends to the Department to 
have a targeted approach in making the four metro blood banks functional at the 
earliest. The Committee would also like to draw the attention of the Department to the 
undue delay in the operationalisation of mode l Blood Bank at Tirupati.  Infrastructure 
for the Blood Bank has already been provided by the State Government. The Secretary 
assured the Committee that action for se nding the equipment for the Blood Bank 
would be taken immediately. 
  
Action Taken 
 
It is submitted that a road-map has been prepared for setting up of Metro 
Blood Banks in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai an d Kolkata following the approval of the 
Cabinet. The requisite land has been made  available by the State Governments of 

West Bengal and Tamil Nadu, while the issue of allotment of land is followed up with 
the State Government of Maharashtra.  
The Design DPR Consultants for prepara tion of Architectural Drawings are 
already in place. The Preliminary Drawings  have already been approved for three 
Metro Blood Bank sites at Kolkata, Chennai and Delhi.  
It is submitted that the construction wo rk for these sites is expected to start 
during the current Financial Year itself. 
In regard to the Model Blood Bank in Tirupati, it is submitted that the proto-
type of equipments to be supplied to this blood bank has already been approved by 
an Expert Committee appointed by NACO. The equipments for the blood bank will be 
supplied and installed during the month of August 2010. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
The Committee observes that the establ ishment of four Metro Blood Banks 
as Centres of Excellence aimed at having four model Blood Banks in Delhi, 
Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata with latest equipments and technology is in its 
third year of conceptualisation but still a lot needs to be done to actually realize the 
same.  Though the Department hopes to start construction on the three sites, the 
issue of land in case of Mumbai is st ill being sorted out. The Committee would 
like to emphasize that the road-map prepared for setting up these Blood Banks 
needs to be adhered to by all concerned, especially the State Implementing 
Agencies. The Committee is not aware abou t the targeted date of completion of 
construction work for these Blood Banks  which is expected to start during the 
current financial year. One must also not fo rget the fact that these Blood Banks can 

be considered fully functional only wh en they are well-equipped having the 
required infrastructure and manpower. As regards the Model Blood Bank in 
Tirupati, the Committee hopes that by no w it would have started functioning as 
per the latest information submitted by the Department. 
VIII  ART CENTERS 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
8.3 The Committee is satisfied that at pres ent the number of patients undergoing 
second line of ART is within the manageab le range. However, the Committee is of the 
considered opinion that the number of cent res of excellence being limited to just 10 
where the patients can have treatment fac ilities, the patients, especially the poor 
people residing far away from theses cent res, will have to spend a lot of money for 
transportation for visiting these centres regularly.  The Committee thinks that with the 
facilities of ART centres expanding, more nu mber of patients requiring second line of 
treatment is going to increase considerably.  Accordingly, the Committee recommends 
to the Department to have a realistic assess ment of the requirement of new Centres of 
Excellence with a view to make the facilitie s for treatment available within reasonable 
distance of the patients. 
Action Taken 
An assessment on the distribution of pa tients referred as “treatment failures” 
and those who were put on 2nd line ART is being done.  Subsequently, ART centres 
will be identified based on volume of eligible cases and capacity to provide 2nd line 
ART.  During 2010-11,  8-10 ART centres will be upgraded through training, provision 

of 2nd line drugs and linkage with viral load  testing facilities.  More centres will be 
upgraded based on volume of patients on 2nd line ART.   
  
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
The Committee appreciates that the Department is undertaking an 
assessment about the distribution of patient s referred as “treatment failures” and 
those who were put on 2nd line ART.  The Committee would like to have the 
details of such assessment as well as of  those ART centres wh ich will be upgraded 
through training, provision of 2nd line drugs and linkage with viral load testing 
facilities during  2010-11. 
IX  NEW INITIATIVES 
Recommendations/Observations 
9.2 The Committee is pained at the slow progress in establishing the National 
Blood Transfusion Authority and setting up of a Plasma Fractionation Plant. Both 
these initiatives are very important. It is very disappointing that the same still remains 
on paper even after two years. The Commi ttee would like to be informed about the 
reasons for the inordinate delay and the de adline by which the same would be set up. 
It recommends to the Department to make  all conceivable efforts to achieve the 
aforesaid targets at the earliest. 
Action Taken 
 
It is submitted that after approval of  the Cabinet, an Expert Committee was 
constituted to finalise adoption of techno logy for this project in view of the highly 
complex technical nature of the project.  The Expert Group has recommended for 
adoption of “Cohn n Chromatography Techno logy” for this project. Subsequently, an 
Expression of Interest was invited from  interested firms to work as Project 

Management Consultant. The process of sele ction of Project Management Consultant 
is in progress. 
In regard to setting up of National Bl ood Transfusion Author ity, the approval 
of Cabinet is under process. The National Blood Transfusion Authority will be set up, 
after approval of the Cabinet on this initiative. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE 
 
The Committee is dismayed at the manner in which establishment of the 
National Blood Transfusion Authority and setting up of a Plasma Fractionation 
Plant is still entangled in paper work. As  both these components are crucial for 
furthering the objectives of NACO, th e Committee had called for reasons for the 
inordinate delay and the deadline by wh ich these two would be set up. Though 
the reply of the Department briefly indicates the progress made so far, nowhere it 
has specified the reasons for the delay or the timelines set by it. In the opinion of 
the Committee this is a case of poor plan ning and implementation strategy on the 
part of the Department. The Committee re commends to the Department to revisit 
its strategy and set out necessary correctiv e measures to achieve these two targets 
at the earliest. 
XII NATIONAL PEDIATRIC INITIATIVE 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
 
12.3 The Committee is very concerned at th e increasing number  of HIV+ children 
and rising trend of HIV prevalence in  pregnant women in low prevalence / 
vulnerable States of North India. However, the Committee considers it to be due to 
Department’s proactive approach in identify ing and tracking the HIV+ mothers or it 

m a y  b e  a n  i n d i c a t i o n  o f  r i s e  o f  t h e  d isease in the low prevalence States.  The 
Committee would recommend to the Department to keep a strict vigil on rising trends 
of HIV prevalence among pregnant wome n in low prevalence States and take 
immediate steps to contain the same.  The Committee may be informed of the specific 
steps taken by the Department in this regard. 
 
12.4 The Committee is pained to imagine the plight of the small children who 
would be requiring the ART treatment in the long run.  The Committee recommends 
to the Department to intensify its approach  to detect the HIV+ children by targeting 
the HIV+ mothers and ensuring full care and support to them.  The Committee may 
be informed about the status of all HIV+ children in India, state-wise. 
  
Action Taken 
 
A  two prong strategy is being implemented to check number of HIV+ children:- 
a) Scale-up identification of HIV+ pregnant women by offering HIV counselling and 
testing routinely at Antenatal Clinics. These identified as HIV+ will be assessed 
for eligibility of ART by performing CD4 count.  This would require better linkage 
between ICTC and ART centres.  Thos e not eligible for ART will be given 
prophylactic treatment.   
b) Follow-up of children exposed to HI V (children born to  HIV+ mother and 
children getting breast feeding from HIV+  mother). They will be identified and 
tested for HIV through latest techno logy (DNA-PCR) for early diagnosis and 
treatment. Active screening of vulnerable children by involving NGOs and 
outreach workers has been initiated. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 

 
  The Committee had called for a status of all HIV+ children in India, State-
wise and had specifically recommended to the Department to keep a strict vigil on 
rising trends of HIV prevalence among pregnant women in low prevalence States 
and, accordingly, had sought details of th e specific steps taken by the Department 
in this regard.  The Department in its response has just reproduced the existing 
procedure being adopted by it. The specif ic information sought by the Committee 
is missing. The Department may, accordingly, provide necessary details in this 
regard.

All India Institute of Ayurveda, New Delhi 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.1.4 The Committee is happy to note the submission  of the Department that there is no change in the e stimates of the project 
and the project is on track and expected to be comp leted within two years from the date of commencement of construction, i.e. , 
May 2010. However, more than two years have already elapsed since the Cabinet approved the project in January, 2008 but the 
designs and plan of construction of the project are  yet to be approved by the Delhi Development Author ity (DDA). Therefore, 
the construction of the building scheduled to commence in 2009-10 itself has been rescheduled for May, 2010. 
Action Taken  
 The Delhi Fire Service, Airport Authority of India , Delhi Urban Art Commission and Delhi Pollution Control Committee 
have conveyed their approval to facilitate final approval of DDA to the construction of building. In the meantime, the contractor 
appointed for construction of the building has move d his manpower and machinery to the construction si te for excavation of 
land before actual construction. 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.1.5 The Committee observes that it is imperative on the part of the Department to vigorously pursue approval of designs and 
drawings of the building with the DDA at the highes t level. The Committee also recommends that the pro gress of the 
construction of the building be monitored at a suff iciently higher level in the Department so that no room is left for time 
overruns and the resultant cost overruns. 
Action Taken  
 The matter is reviewed regularly at the level of S ecretary (AYUSH) so as to expedite implementation o f the project and 
minimize time and cost overruns.

medicals required for upgradation of the Hospital. The Committee finds that only 20 Ayurvedic Medical Officers have joined so 
far. The Committee is not aware about the status of  para-medical personnel. Posts of Medical Superintendent of the Hospital is 
yet to be filled. In such a scenario, the Committee  can only conclude that the CGHS Ayurveda Hospital cannot be considered 
fully functional as the Hospital is yet to be equip ped with both required infrastructure and manpower.  The Committee once 
again enjoins upon the Department to make all effor ts so as to ensure the outreach of envisaged health  care to the targeted 
beneficiaries.

been taken for filling up the vacant posts of Medic al Officers in the Hospital. So far, 22 newly recru ited Medical Officers have 
joined the Department/ CGHS out of which 4 Medical Officers have been posted in Ayurvcdic Hospital by CGHS. As such, 
against the sanctioned strength (pre-upgradation fr om 25 bed to 50 bedded Hospital) of 9 Doctors/ Spec ialists, 6 have been 
posted in the Hospital. 

 Action for filling up the vacancies of Medical Off icer (AY) on ‘direct recruitment’ basis through UPS C will be initiated 
after ascertaining the overall vacancy position in the Hospitals/ Dispensaries of CGHS. Meanwhile, it is proposed to engage

the post of MS.

North-Eastern Institute of Ayurveda and Homoeopathy, Shillong 
Recommendations/Observations  
5.5.4 The Committee views with serious concern the tardy progress made in the operationalisation of a national level Institute of 
AYUSH system of health-care in the much-needed N-E region of the country. The Committee would like to point out that the 
total cost of the first phase of the project is est imated at Rs.67.50 crore. The Committee wonders as to how far the Task Force 
headed by the Secretary (AYUSH) constituted for imp lementation of the project would prove to be helpfu l. The Committee 
does not have much hope even in the first phase of the project taking off by the end of Eleventh Plan. With reported expenditure 
of only Rs. 9.00 crore upto 2009-10 and proposed pr ovision of Rs.17.00 crore for 2010-11, one can draw  the very obvious 
conclusion. The Committee apprehends that chances o f there being both time-overruns and cost-overruns are very much there. 
The Committee can only emphasize that the Task Force has to vigorously supervise the implementation of first phase of NEIAH 
at Shillong, identifying the problem areas along with simultaneously moving for removal of the same. Only then, this ambitious 
project would succeed in becoming functional in the real sense. 
Action Taken  
 Implementation of the project picked up with vigor ous follow up of the matter with the Project Management Consultants, 
M/s HSCC (India) Limited. The contractor for constr uction of the building has been appointed and the c ontractor has already 
moved his manpower and machinery to the constructio n site for commencement of the construction. Constr uction of the 
building has commenced in October, 2010. 
 In the meantime, the Director of the Institute has  been appointed with effect from 2.6.2010. He has s tarted functioning 
from Shillong. The project is expected to complete well in time. As regards the apprehension of the Committee about utilization 
of funds, it is submitted that actual expenditure would increase with the pace of construction. 
 

North Eastern Institute of Folk Medicine, Passighat, Arunachal Pradesh 
Recommendations/Observations  
5.6.2  Eleventh Plan outlay for the Institute was R s.41.00 crore. Although Rs.16.69 crore were allocat ed during the first three 
years of the Plan period, Institute continues to be  at a proposal stage. As a result allocated funds r emained unutilized. While 
trying to assess the different stages of preparatory exercise for starting the Institute, the Committee is surprised to note that after 
the Cabinet approval in February, 2008, it took ful l one year (2008-09) for appointing the Project Con sultant, i.e. , M/s HSCC 
and getting the required land. However, both the actions had to undergo a drastic change. M/s HLL took the place of M/s HSCC 
as Project Consultant. Issue of allotment of disputed land ultimately got the necessary clearance from the concerned authorities. 
As a result, another year passed with the project continuing to be at the proposal stage. The Committee is constrained to observe 
that due care was not taken in both the selection o f Project Consultant and selection of Project site by all the concerned 
agencies. The Committee apprehends that the initial  estimated cost of Rs.32.88 crore for the Project w ould undoubtedly 
undergo a drastic enhancement. 
Action Taken  
 The project of the North Eastern Institute of Folk  Medicine, Passighat was got delayed a little due t o delay in transfer of 
the forest land by the State Govt. The State Forest  Department kept the transfer of land pending due t o non-payment of the 
diversion cost of the land by the State Health Depa rtment. As per the agreement, the cost of the land is to be borne by the State 
Govt. However, in order to expedite transfer of lan d, the environmental impact study of the land was d one and drawings and 
designs of the building taken up by the Project Management Consultants, M/s HLL Lifecare Limited. Now, the prbj6ct is in full 
swing. Tenders have been issued and contractor has been finalized. The actual work commenced from August, 2010. 
 After careful planning and tactful handling of the  project at senior level and continuous monitoring, it has been possible to 
keep the project cost within the limit of the initi al cost. Hence, it is expected that there will be n o cost escalation in the project 
cost. 
Recommendations/Observations  
5.6.3  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the remaining approvals and pre-construction activities may be expedited so 
that construction of the building is started within the first half of 201 0-11. For this, the Project Monitoring Committee will have 
to be constantly on alert. The Committee desires to  be apprised of the necessary steps taken and the m odalities worked out to 
ensure completion of the project on time and also check cost overruns of the project. (Para 5.6.3) 
Action Taken  
 The Project Monitoring Committee headed by Secreta ry (AYUSH) is constantly monitoring the project. The Government 
has appointed a senior IAS Officer, belonging to the region, as Director of the Institution. It would help better coordination with 
the local administration and State Government authorities.

the agencies concerned. If it takes almost three ye ars for the Department to finalize recruitment rule s for the posts and 
get necessary approvals from local authorities, it is a sad commentary on its functioning and calls in to question its 
seriousness of exercising fiscal prudence. Now that all the groundwork has been completed, the Committee would expect 
the Department to monitor the progress in respect o f all items of work meticulously and come up with s ubstantive 
achievements in this regard. 
Setting up of National Board for Medicinal Plants

coordinating all matters relating to medicinal plan ts and support policies and programmes for growth o f trade, export, 

conservation and cultivation of medicinal plants. D espite the above fact, only Rs. 40.00 crore could b e made available 
out of a provision of Rs. 50.00 crore made in BE 20 09-10. Taking note of the fact that the expenditure  under this head 
was Rs. 39.19 crore as on 15th March, 2010, the Com mittee is pretty certain that the entire allocation  under this head 
must have been utilized by the end of the financial  year 2009-10. The Committee observes that while th ere have been 
recurrent savings under some of the heads with the budgeted amount being surrended year after year, su ch an 
important initiative as setting up of NMPB had to s uffer financial crunch due to skewed priorities of the Department. 
The Committee would, therefore, tend to infer that there was something wrong with prioritizing policy of Department of 
AYUSH and impress upon it to be more careful in this regard.  
CGHS Ayurveda Hospital and Educational Institutions

utilize the same. The Committee would like the Depa rtment to ascertain the reasons for the same from C PWD and

afford to continue with slow-moving mindset of yest erday. The Committee would also like the Department  to address 
the issue of non-filling up of vacant posts with a renewed vigor and apprise it of the progress made in this regard.

VI.  RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT 
Recommendations/Observations  
6.6 Committee’s attention has been drawn by some re ports about successful treatment of Cancer patients by Ayurvedic drugs. 
On a specific query about the veracity of these rep orts, the Committee was pleasantly surprised to not e the significant 
achievements made by the Ayurvedic practitioners as indicated below:- 
- On the recommendation of the Scientific Advisory Committee (Ayurveda), the CCRAS has initiated the s tudy of 
‘CARCTOL’ a proprietary medicine of Vaid Nand Lal Tiwari of Jaipur supposed to have anti-cancer properties. For 
verifying the therapeutic claim, standardization work has been completed by the Council. Safety and toxicity studies 
have also been completed. As informed by the Ex. Director-General, CCRAS, ‘CARCTOL’ has also been subjected 
to in-vitro study at Advanced Cancer Research Centr e of TATA, Mumbai against 14 types of human cancer cells 
out of which it was found effective against pancrea tic and lung cancer. It was placed on record that C ARCTOL is 
being used for treatment of cancer: patients both i n the country and abroad. After preparation of doss iers, multi-
centric clinical trials will be conducted. 
-  Pre-clinical study of ‘Cancer Gaza Kesari’ a pro prietary drug of Vaid Krishan Gopal of Ajmer has al so been 
conducted by the Council in collaboration with Vete rinary College, Chennai. The study revealed that th e drug 
significantly reduced the mammary tumor incidence, latency, frequency, rate of growth and malignancy. It was also 
subjected to in-vitro study against 14 types of hum an cancer cell line, out of which it has shown to b e of effect 
against Pancreatic and Lung Cancer. 
-  Pilot project was sanctioned by the Ministry in 1996 to study the effects of metal based formulatio ns prepared by 
Vaid Balendu Prakash of Dehradun in the treatment of Acute pro-myllolic Leukemia. The Committee was informed 
that the drug was patented jointly by the Council w ith Germany. The Committee was also given to unders tand the 
Vaid Balendu Prakash has been treating Cancer patie nts with the drug. On a specific qucry it was clari fied that the 
Indo-German patent was a process patent. So far onl y a pilot study of 21 patients has been conducted b y the 
Council. Multi- Cultural Clinical Trials of the drug were to be undertaken which would take four years. 
-  The Committee also notes that ethical approval a nd release of funds for clinical trial of AYUSH QOL-2C at AIIMS 
has been completed. Registration of patent is to be initiated shortly. Simultaneously, 10 patients have been enrolled 
for study at St. Johns Medical College, Bangalore. This drug is reported to improve quality of life of those receiving 
chemotherapy /radiotherapy. 
Action Taken  
 The encouraging observations of the august committ ee have been noted.  

Recommendations/Observations  
6.7 The Committee places on record its appreciation  of commendable work being done by the Research Cou ncils on their 
own and also in collaboration with well-known institutions in the country and abroad. Work of the CCRAS touches both routine 
ailments as well as chronic ailments where permanen t cure is yet to be found inspite of giant strides made by the modern 
medical sciences. In such a scenario, for the treat ment of the most deadly cancer disease, any signifi cant achievement by any 
system of medicine should be welcome to all. The ‘C ommittee considers it a strange irony that although  large number of 
patients are getting relief by the drugs formulated by individuals after years of their single-handed research, official recognition 
still remains elusive to them. The Committee strong ly advocates the streamlining and expediting of the  official certification 
process, so that humanity at large gets the long-awaited relief. 
Action Taken  
 Whenever any claim is submitted to Council, the sa me are examined and put before Scientific Advisory Committee to 
carry out scientific validation. In this context, t wo claims on cancer have been subjected to Pre-clin ical Studies based on which 
clinical trial will be carried out as per lead. If any drug is finally marketed, the benefit will be s hared by Council and the 
claimant. But there is no provision of Certification by the Council. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
 The Committee is not satisfied with the evasive re ply given by the Department. Keeping in view that t here is no 
effective cure/treatment for cancer in the modern s ystem of medicines, the Department should make all out efforts to 
exploit any significant achievement by any system o f medicine towards treatment/cure of such a deadly disease. The 
adequate and effective mechanism should be in place  to expedite scientific validation of any claim in this regard. The 
Committee notes with dismay that the Department has  failed so far in carrying out-scientific validatio n of such claims 
due to procedural delays and lack of adequate resea rch work and expertise in this regard. The Committe e would 
reiterate once again that the process of clinical t rial on two claims of cancer needs to start at the earliest. Contention of 
the Department that in the event of any drug being finally marketed, the benefit would be shared by the Council and the 
claimant, does not lead to the ultimate goal of pro viding relief to patients suffering from cancer. It  is a well-known fact 
that this disease is spreading at an alarming rate with new dimensions emerging. In such a scenario, t he Department 
along with the Research Council needs to play a pro-active role.

IX.  QUALITY CONTROL OF AYUSH DRUGS 
Recommendations/Observations  
9.1 The AYUSH system of medicine is governed by Dru gs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules made thereunder. Enforcement 
provision of Chapter IV A of Drugs & Cosmetics Act,  1940 is the responsibility of State Governments. E stablishment of State 
Drug Testing Laboratories is also a statutory responsibility of States under the Act. To provide financial assistance to States for 
strengthening enforcement mechanism, the Drug Quali ty Control Scheme was started in IXth plan. Over th e years, 29 State 
Drug Testing Laboratories and 46 State Pharmacies h ave been set up and upgraded @ Rs.1.50 crore/DTI, a nd Rs. 2.00 
crore/pharmacy. In the Eleventh plan the scheme was  revised to include three new components of strengt hening of the State 
enforcement mechanism, upgrading the in-house testi ng facilities of manufacturing units and assisting manufacturing units 
desirous of obtaining higher GMP like EU and WHO-GMP. 
9.2  The Committee notes that inspite of major chan ges in the scheme, fund utilization status has been  far from satisfactory. 
Against an Eleventh Plan outlay of Rs.225 crore, fu nds amounting to only Rs. 45.00 crore could be allo cated during the first 
three years of the plan period and expenditure reported upto 15th March, 2010 is only Rs.26.52 crore. 

9.3  The Committee finds that out of 29 Drug Testin g Laboratories assisted financially so far, 17 labs  are established in terms 
of equipment and buildings. Other labs are in diffe rent stages of construction of building and procure ment of equipment. Only 
46 ASU&H pharmacies have been covered under the Scheme so far. 
9.4 Committee’s attention has also been drawn by th e very low number of GMP compliant ASU&H Drug manuf acturing 
units in the country. Out of total 9837 such units,  only 4663 units are GMP complying units. Ratio of GMP compliant /non-
GMP compliant units is very unsatisfactory with the  maximum gap noticed in States like Assam, Haryana,  Kerala, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, U.P., Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand , Punjab. As many as 2336 legal notices have been i ssued/licenses 
cancelled so far. 
9.5 The Committee has taken note of a number of cor rective measures suggested during the Mid-term Appr aisal of Eleventh 
plan. The Committee would like to emphasize that qu ality control and quality assurance are the major i ssues with reference to 
ASU drugs. The Committee, therefore, recommends tha t corrective measures as suggested in the Mid-term Appraisal may be 
initiated without delay. 
Action Taken  
 Mid term appraisal was done for the Centrally Spon sored Scheme for Quality Control of ASU&H drugs for  the effective 
implementation of the scheme. A meeting was held on  15.10.09 in the Planning Commission. Under the sch eme Rs. 2.30 erore 
has been spent till now. Other corrective measures are being taken for effective implementation. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
 This is yet another instance of casual reply by th e Department. Instead of furnishing a comprehensive  reply 
detailing the specific measures being taken/contemplated to be taken towards overcoming the shortcomings as identified 
in the mid-term appraisal, the Department has merely made a generic statement which, in the opinion of the Committee, 
is tantamount to being evasive. The Committee, acco rdingly, recommends to the Department to shed more light on the 
measures being taken for addressing the shortcoming s, especially those concerning quality control and quality 
assurance.

Homoeopathic (ASU & H) drugs are not being complied  with strictly. The Committee feels that the absenc e of proper labeling 
on ASU & H drugs may be a cause of health hazards. The Committee therefore, recommends that the monitoring mechanism in 
this regard be streamlined to ensure proper labeling on ASU & H drugs.

 Chapters IV A of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act 1940 and Rules 1945 have been enforced. The responsibili ty of State

AYUSH is also reviewing the status position for the  implementation and enforcement of the Chapters IV A or the Drugs and

have also been issued for stick compliance of labeling provision on ASU&H drugs by the State Licensing Authorities. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
 The Committee is well aware that compliance of labe ling provision on AYUSH drugs as mandated under the

vacancies and the outcome of efforts made towards filling up of those vacancies.   (Para 8.8)  
 The Committee notes that the Department has detail ed the decisions taken by NMPB in its meeting held on 10th 
July, 2007. However, nothing has been mentioned about the follow-up action taken thereon, though more than three and 
a half years have passed since then. This silence i s all the more baffling in view of the fact that NM PB itself felt in 2007 
that strengthening of State Medicinal Plants Boards is key to proper implementation and monitoring of the project. The 
Department should have acted like a catalyst and en sured forward movement in the matter; instead, it h as chosen to 
remain silent on the issue, which is deplorable. Th e Committee would, therefore, like to be apprised o f the steps taken / 
being taken towards implementing the various decisions taken regarding strengthening of SMPBs.   (Para 8.9)  
IX.   QUALITY CONTROL OF AYUSH DRUGS 
 This is yet another instance of casual reply by th e Department. Instead of furnishing a comprehensive  reply 
detailing the specific measures being taken/contemplated to be taken towards overcoming the shortcomings as identified 
in the mid-term appraisal, the Department has merely made a generic statement which, in the opinion of the Committee, 
is tantamount to being evasive. The Committee, acco rdingly, recommends to the Department to shed more light on the 
measures being taken for addressing the shortcoming s, especially those concerning quality control and quality 
assurance.      (Paras 9.1, 9.2, 9.3,9.4 & 9.5)  
 The Committee is well aware that compliance of lab eling provision on AYUSH drugs as mandated under th e 
Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules made thereu nder is the responsibility of State Drug Licensing Authorities. 
Merely writing to the State Governments in this reg ard from time to time will not ensure the complianc e of this very 
crucial condition. The Committee has been repeatedl y emphasizing the need for having an effective moni toring 

mechanism for quality control of AYUSH drugs both w ith the objective of protecting the consumers’ inte rest as well as 
propagation of this alternative system of medicine.   (Para 9.6)  
X.  AYUSH PHARMACEUTICAL INDUSTRY 
Indian, Medicine Pharmaceutical Corporation Limited (IMPCL) 
 The Committee welcomes the much awaited approval o f the 3rd phase of modernization of the Indian Medi cine 
Pharmaceutical Corporation Limited (IMPCL). The Com mittee hopes that implementation of this project wi ll be 
accomplished in a time-bound manner.   (Para 10.3)  
XI.  DEVELOPMENT OF COMMON FACILITIES FOR THE AYUSH IND USTRY CLUSTERS 
 The Committee is constrained to observe that the r eply of the Department is full of ambiguity. Instea d of 
unraveling various dimensions of under-utilization of the funds in unambiguous terms, the Department h as sought to 
prevaricate. For example, the Committee was earlier  informed by the Department that the allocation of Rs. 25.00 crore 
in BE 2009-10 was brought down to Rs. 10.00 at RE s tage due to reduced allocation as a whole for the D epartment. The 
Department has now informed that allocation had to be reduced to Rs. 10.00 at RE stage due to inadequa te proposals 
received during the 1st half. The Committee would t herefore, like the Department to explain this ambig uity. The 
Committee also notes that against the utilization f igures of Rs. 8.57 crore as on 15th March, 2010, th e funds released 
upto 31st March, 2010 amounted to Rs. 16.54 crore. The Committee would, like the Department to indicat e the 
proposals received for funding under this head and the amount released for them, month-wise.   (Para 11.2)  
XII.  SURVEY ON USAGE AND ACCEPTABILITY OF AYUSII 
 The Department has chosen to remain silent on the issue of how the funds to the tune of Rs. 66 lakhs have been 
spent when no agency was finalised to conduct the survey. The Committee would like to be apprised on this account.  
       (Para 12.3)  
XIII.   DEVELOPMENT OF INSTITUTIONS 
 The Committee observes that modifications in the e ligibility criteria for releasing grants-in-aid to AYUSH 
Educational Institutions is a positive initiative t aken by the Department. The Committee would appreci ate if all the 
procedural formalities for approval of the Scheme are completed at the earliest.   (Para 13.4)  
XV.  INTERNATIONAL COOPERATION 
 The Depart{Dent has not indicated any forward move ment made by the Advisory Committee set up under th e 
Chairmanship of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar. The Committee desires to be kept apprised of the progress made by the Advisory 
Committee.             (Para 15.2)

II.  BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.10   Committee’s attention has also been drawn by  unspent balances lying with a number of Institutio ns. As on 1st 
December, 2009, maximum unspent balances amounting to Rs. 28.79 crore, Rs. 36.52 crore and Rs. 80.43 c rore were reported 
against the North-Eastern Indira Gandhi Regional Institute of Health and Medical Sciences, Shillong, LGB Regional Institute of 
Mental Health, Tezpur, Assam and AIIMS, New Delhi. Except AIIMS, the other two Institutes had unspent balances as on 1st 
April, 2009. Reasons for availability of such a hug e amount of unspent balances are not known to the C ommittee. However, 
such a state of affairs in national level institute s is indeed a cause  of concern for the Committee. This clearly shows that some 
major activities both ongoing/proposed might be adv ersely affected. The Committee would appreciate if the matter is taken up 
with the concerned authorities without further delay. 
Action Taken  
  The Department shares the concern of the Hon’ble Committee and has made it clear to the Institutions  concerned that 
further fund releases will depend on the pace of liquidation of their unspent balances. 
Recommendations/Observations  
2.13   The Committee notes that as a further effort  to maximize liquidation of UCs, a communication has been sent by the 
Secretary (Health) to the Principal Health Secretaries of all the States. If need be, this exercise ne eds to be pursued further with 
higher authorities. 
Action Taken  
  A D.O. letter at the level of Secretary (Health) is being issued to all the Chief Secretaries of the  States concerned after 
compilation of State-wise data pertaining to the grants released upto 31.03.2009. 
IV.   SAFDARJUNG  HOSPITAL  AND VARDHMAN MAHAVEER M EDICAL COLLEGE, NEW DELHI 
Recommendations/Observations  
4.2   The Committee notes that against projected Pl an requirement of Rs. 180.60 crore for 2010-11 for the Hospital, allocation 
of Rs. 118.60 crore has been made. Given the fact t hat out of the RE plan allocation of Rs. 129.92 cro re for 2009-10, the 
Hospital was able to spend Rs. 112.76 crore upto 28th February, 2010, with every possibility of full utilization by the end of the 
year, the Committee is unable to comprehend the rea sons behind a huge gap of Rs. 62.00 crore between t he projected and 
budgeted funds for 2010-11. The Committee, therefor e, recommends that additional funds be allocated fo r the Hospital at RE 
stage so that lack of funds should not hamper the re-developmental activities undertaken by the Hospital. 
Action Taken  
  Noted for compliance.

XVIII. MEDICAL EDUCATION 
Recommendations/Observations  
18.4  The Committee is not inclined to agree with t he Department’s view that all is well with the exis ting procedure for 
recognition of MBBS degree colleges. The Department  cannot escape from its responsibility by citing th at it is the 
responsibility of the individual colleges to seek r ecognition. The Committee opines that the Departmen t needs to have into 
consideration the psychological impact of such a si tuation on the final year students who in its opini on would be more anxious 
to see their college getting recognition rather than taking their examinations seriously. The Committee is of the considered view 
that the whole procedure of recognition should be c omplete well before the final year students take th eir examinations. The 
Committee therefore recommends to the Department to  revisit its stand on the issue and come up with so me concrete steps. A 
status note on the issue of recognition to 15 medic al colleges where the first batches of MBBS student s have appeared for final 
examination in the academic year 2010 may be furnished. 
Action Taken  
  As per the provisions of MCI Regulations on Estab lishment of medical colleges, permission to establish a medical college 
and admit students is granted initially for a perio d of one year and is renewed on yearly basis subjec t to verification of 
achievements of annual targets. It is the responsibility of the person to apply to the MCI for purpose of renewal six months prior 
to the expiry of the initial permission. The MCI ca rries out inspections for annual renewal of permiss ion till such time the 
establishment of the Medical College and expansion of the hospital facilities are complete and a forma l recognition of the 
medical qualification of the college is granted. 
  The Committee’s view to complete whole procedure of recognition well before the final year student t ake their 
examination is appreciated. It will take some time to review the procedure of recognition as it requir es consultation with 
Medical Council of India. 
  Present status of 15 medical colleges where first  batch of MBBS students has appeared for final examination but are yet to 
be recognized in the academic year 2010 as on 14.5.2010 is at Annexure-XII . 
Recommendations/Observations  

18.7   The Committee is in full agreement with the initiatives proposed by the Dental Council of India (DCI) especially in 
view of the fact that so many seats are lying vacant year after year. Further, the Committee is of the firm opinion that education 
and accordingly the number of seats should be need based and keeping in view the demand and supply sce nario. Here, by the 
figures available with the Committee, it is amply clear that there is an urgent need for intervention to balance the same. In view 
of the above, the Committee recommends to the Depar tment to take some urgent steps in consultation wit h the DCI and the 
various State Governments, so that this unwanted trend is arrested at the earliest and precious resources are utilized purposefully 
in other areas of medical education. The Committee also recommends to the Department to actively consi der the proposal 
submitted to it by the DCI regarding making norms of opening new college more stringent. 
Action Taken  
  The DCI Regulations governing the establishment o f new dental colleges are made stringent and are be ing changed 
suitably viz . 
a.  Essentiality certificate from the State Governm ent with a statement that in case the applicant fai ls to create 
infrastructure for the dental college, fresh admiss ion will be stopped and the State Government shall take over the 
responsibility of the students already admitted in the college with the permission of the Central Government. 
b.  University affiliation from the concerned Unive rsity. 
c.  Attachment with own 100 bedded General Hospital / Government General Hospital/Medical College with a radius 
of 10 kms. 
d.  Accreditation of dental colleges by the externa l agency.

3.25   Though the Committee appreciates Department’ s initiative for ensuring quality service to CGHS b eneficiaries and 
has no doubts over the professionalism of NABH/NABL , yet it does not find much merit in making it comp ulsory as a 
precondition for empanelment under CGHS. The NABL/N ABH lay down certain norms and standards to be obse rved and on 
inspection, they provide accreditation to those who  fulfil the said standards. There is no guarantee t hat once accredited, the 
Hospital/diagnostic centre will maintain those standards till the next inspection by NABL/NABH. Further, it has been observed 
that many of the reputed hospitals don’t go for acc reditation under them. In such a scenario it may be  counterproductive as the 
beneficiaries may be deprived of services under suc h reputed Hospitals/diagnostic centres. The Committ ee accordingly 
recommends to the Department to be cautious on this move. 
3.26   The Committee would also like to have inform ation regarding the number of NABH/NABL accredited Government 
hospitals/diagnostic centres as well as private hospitals/diagnostic centres empanelled under CGHS. 
Action Taken  
  When the CGHS initiated and completed the process  of empanelment of private hospitals and diagnostic  centres during 
2004, the so called big hospitals acted pricey and did not accept the rates arising out of tender proc ess. CGHS was left with no 
option but to empanel only those hospitals and diag nostic centres which accepted the package rates. CG HS has no power to 
compulsorily empanel hospitals and diagnostic centr es under it. After the completion of empanelment pr ocess, considerable 
doubts were expressed in various forums that CGHS e mpanelled “fly-by night operators” and “big hospita ls have been 
eliminated from the tendering process”. One point that no one appreciated was that CGHS had prescribed the parameters for the 
hospitals and diagnostic centres to fulfil before e mpanelment and also that the empanelment orders wer e not issued without the 
specific recommendation of the Quality Council of I ndia. Quality Council of India (QCI) is an organisa tion set up by the 
Ministry of Commerce and Industry. A team of QCI wo uld physically inspect the premises of the hospital s and diagnostic 
centres to confirm that they conformed to the param eters fixed by the CGHS, and only those hospitals a nd diagnostic centres 
were recommended to the CGHS for empanelment as wer e fulfilling the prescribed conditions. In addition , the hospitals and 
diagnostic centres were required to submit bank guarantees and sign MOA with CGHS, which had stringent conditions. 
  The criticism of CGHS of ignoring “big” hospitals  continues even today though on a slightly muted condition. 
  According to QCI, accreditation is a process base d on a system implemented across the organisation. It has to be practiced 
by its management, staff, clients (patients) all the time and being continuously monitored, leaving no room for relaxation of the 
requirements. Moreover, it is a process adopted by the management with an aim to improve its services.  It is different from an 
inspection which is based on the verification of in frastructure on fixed time basis. Therefore, accred itation mechanism is 
entirely different from the inspection. Accreditati on body also monitors the performance of .its accre dited facilities on a 
continuous basis by way of on-site surveillance ass essments, renewal assessments, off-site monitoring using data on various 
indicators, verifying complaints from users of the services, etc. Thus, a hospital once accredited doe s not mean that it will 
remain accredited forever. NABH can suspend or with draw accreditation on various grounds laid down in its policies and 
known to accredited hospitals. Patient safety and qualify of care are cardinal points in the accreditation. The accredited hospital 
needs to establish systems, processes and more impo rtantly monitor key clinical outcomes. All major gr oups of hospital 
industry, i.e.  Apollo, Fortis, Max Wockhardt, Columbia Asia, Narayana Hrudalaya, etc., have adopted NABH accreditation. 

  Unlike regulation, accreditation is voluntary. Ac creditation is driven by market forces, empanelling  and paying agencies. 
It stands to logic that paying agency has the right  to demand quality and the CGHS has taken the appro priate decision to 
demand accreditation so as to provide safe healthcare to its beneficiaries. 
  Presently, 45 private and 2 Government hospitals have been accredited by NABH and there are over 400  applications for 
accreditation which are under different stages of evaluation for accreditation. Over 70 hospitals have undergone pre-assessment 
and now working towards final assessment. Over 20 h ospitals have undergone final assessment and now wo rking to close the 
deficiencies so that case can be put to the Accredi tation Committee for recommendation. It is a dynami c process and the 
statistics keep changing as hospitals keep moving from one step to another. 
  It is learnt that after the CGHS imposed the cond ition of accreditation with NABH / NABL for empanel ment under it, 
QCI received over 300 applications for accreditation, which proves that private hospitals and diagnostic centres need CGHS for 
their profitability as much as CGHS wants them to s erve its beneficiaries. The condition will, in the long run, prove beneficial 
to the welfare of CGHS beneficiaries, which is a win-win situation for CGHS.

21.4   The Committee is happy with the introduction  of such a policy tendering monetary award to infor mers providing 
information about the spurious drugs. The Committee  would like to be apprised of the details of the po licy along with any 
achievement made so far under the policy.  
Action Taken  
  Whistle Blower Scheme ––  Whistle Blower Scheme has been devised by the cent ral Government for giving monetary 
rewards to the Whistle Blower who can take risk of providing the information about the perpetrators fo r such crimes. The 
Reward scheme provides for giving handsome rewards to the informers who provides specific information to the designated 
authorities leading to the seizures of spurious, adulterated, misbranded and not of standard quality drugs, cosmetics and medical 
devices. This reward scheme will be applicable to both the informers as well as the officers of the Government and CDSCO. 
  The Additional secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has issued letters to all Chief Secr etaries of States/UTs 
on 14th October 2009 with the request for the wide publicity of the Scheme. 
  As per the Whistle Blower Policy, the reward of m aximum of upto 20% of the total cost of consignment s seized will be 
payable to the informer / officials which should no t in any case exceed Rs.25 Lakh in each case. 25% o f the amount will be 
payable to the whistle blower at the time of filing  of complaint in the court of law, 25% at the time of disposal of the case in 
favour of the Government and the rest of the amount, that is, 50% when the case is finally decided and the matter is not pending 
in any court of law in the country. The eligibility  of the informer and the quantum of cash rewards wo uld be decided by a 
Committee, which will consist of officials from different departments / offices. To ensure speedy trials of the cases, these cases 
will be filed before the Designated / Special Court s set up for the purposes of drugs related issues a s per the provisions of the 
Drugs and Cosmetics (Amendment) Act, 2008. 
  Drug Controller General (India) along with other officials will be the nodal authority who will inter alia  oversee the 
functioning of the Reward Scheme as proposed herein above. 
  The Zonal and Sub-Zonal officers of the CDSCO wil l act as the nodal officer to whom the whistle blow er/informer can 
provide the information about the manufacture /movement of spurious /adultered drugs. 
  The identity of the whistle blower/informer will be kept secret and will be known only to the Nodal Officers, i.e. 
concerned zonal and sub-zonal officers of the CDSCO , the DCG (1) and the Director General Health Servi ces. It will be the 
responsibility of the concerned officials to keep the details of the whistle blower / informer secret. 
  On receipt of the information from a whistle blow er/informer, the concerned Nodal officers will orga nize immediate and 
systematic investigation in co-ordination with the State Drugs Control Administration to unearth the spurious drugs racket. 
  The details of the investigations will then be fo rwarded by the concerned zonal/sub-zonal officer to  the DCG (I) for the 
consideration of the committee to decide about the merit of the case for reward and the quantum of rew ard to be given to the 
whistle blower / informer. 
  The CDSCO has received so far 27 cases from the d ifferent parts of the country, however in some case s complaints were 
repeated as they were received twice and some of the cases were found to be fictitious, Rest of the cases are under investigation. 

The details of the current status on the Whistle Bl ower Policy as on 30th April 2010 are at Annexure-XVI  for your kind 
perusal. 
  No reward under the scheme has been offered as th e first instalment has to be given after launching of prosecution in the 
court of Law.

Recommendations/Observations  
2.7   The Committee is dismayed at the fact that it s continuous concerns and recommendations to the De partment to put a 
proper mechanism in place for - presenting its case for fund requirement before the Planning Commission in a realistic manner, 
and to arrest the trend of under utilization of funds seem to have failed to make any impact. Atleast the Department needs to try 
some innovative methods to achieve optimum utilization of funds. Health is a crucial sector for the allround development of the 
nation and accordingly the Committee has been advoc ating higher allocation of funds for this sector ev ery year. But with the 
Department itself admitting to the slow pace of exp enditure in respect of many schemes/programmes init iated by it, the 
Committee finds advocacy for additional funds servi ng no purpose. The Committee, therefore, recommends  to the Department 
to undertake a comprehensive analysis of the trend of expenditure for the past three years with a view  to identifying the 
underlying causes of underutilization. Such an exer cise should enable the Department to not only impro ve the utilization level 
of the budgeted funds but also to improve upon the existing system of assessing requirement of funds. The Committee is also of 
the opinion that the Department needs to take up wi th the implementing agencies as and when schemes ar e found not being 
implemented as per the Action Plan.

  The Department examines critically each proposal before arriving at the requirement of budgetary allocations for the plan. 
The Department assesses the fund requirement based on the several factors like expenditure trends of e ach 
scheme/programme/institution, status of New Schemes - whether EFC/SFC has been prepared or not, finaliz ation of tendering 
process in respect of construction activities, proc urement of Machines and Equipments, etc. The requir ements of outlay are 
conveyed to the Planning Commission for approval. H owever, it is the jurisdiction of the Planning Comm ission to decide the 
plan outlay for the Ministries/Departments based on  the overall resources available and priorities dec ided by the Planning 
Commission. 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE  
  The Committee had urged upon the Department to unde rtake a comprehensive analysis of the trend of 
expenditure for the past three years with a view to improve the utilization level of the budgeted funds as also to improve 
upon the existing system of assessing requirement o f funds. However, the Committee is constrained to o bserve that the 
Department’s response has been outrightly evasive in as much as it has reproduced its existing procedure of examination 
of funds requirement. The onus of providing Plan Ou tlay has been solely put on the Planning Commission . The 
Committee opines that if the utilisation of funds had been sub-optimal, how it can expect allocation of enhanced amount 
of funds from the Planning Commission for its vario us programmes/policies/schemes. The Committee finds that sincere 
efforts are lacking on the part of the Department i n this direction. No innovative or new strategy, as  exhorted by the 
Committee, seems to have been worked out by it. In such a scenario, the Committee does not hope any positive change in 

this regard if the Department’s approach remains un changed. The Committee, therefore, recommends to th e 
Department to put forth concerted efforts to convince the Planning Commission for allocation of adequate funds.
